1 Lesson 1 of 12 · A1 Kinematics
Distance, displacement & acceleration
How do we describe motion precisely? Learn the difference between distance and displacement, master scalars vs vectors, and see how acceleration links changes in velocity to time.

🚗 Hook – The New York–Boston paradox

A family drives from New York City to Boston. Their car’s odometer reads 384 km. However, a straight line on a map shows only 300 km. Which number is the distance travelled, and which is the displacement? How can two different measurements describe the same trip? Understanding this distinction is the first step to analysing motion in physics.

Fig 1 — Travel distance (curved road) 384 km vs displacement (straight arrow) 300 km northeast.
💡 Diagnostic question (think – then click) — If a runner completes one lap of a 400 m track and returns to the start, what are the distance and displacement? Answer: distance = 400 m, displacement = 0 m (because final position = initial position).

📐 Scalars, vectors, and the difference between distance and displacement

Scalars have only magnitude (size). Examples: mass, time, speed, distance. Vectors have both magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force.

Distance is the total length of a path travelled – a scalar. Displacement is the straight‑line distance from a reference point in a specified direction – a vector.

Distance (scalar) & displacement (vector) $$s_{\text{distance}} = \text{total path length} \qquad \vec{s}_{\text{disp}} = \text{final position} - \text{initial position}$$
Fig 2 — A 4 km walk returns to start → total distance = 4 km, final displacement = 0.

⏱️ Speed, velocity & measuring motion

Speed = distance / time (scalar). Velocity = displacement / time (vector). Average values are over a finite time; instantaneous values are measured over an infinitesimally small interval (e.g., from a light gate).

Average speed & average velocity $$v_{\text{avg speed}} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\Delta t} \qquad \vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{s}}{\Delta t}$$

Human reaction times (~0.25 s) introduce uncertainty when using stopwatches. Light gates provide precise timing by detecting when a beam is interrupted.

Fig 3 — Measuring reaction time: catch a falling ruler; distance fallen gives time from \(s = 5t^2\).
Fig 4 — Air track & light gate: speed = card length / time through gate (instantaneous approximation).

📈 Acceleration – changing velocity

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. It is a vector. Speeding up, slowing down (deceleration), and changing direction are all forms of acceleration. Uniform acceleration means constant magnitude and direction.

Definition of acceleration $$a = \frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t} = \frac{v - u}{t} \quad (\text{SI unit: } \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}})$$

If acceleration is opposite to velocity (negative sign), speed decreases. In everyday language we call this deceleration.

💡 Example: A train slows from \(84\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to rest in 60 s → \(a = (0-84)/60 = -1.4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The negative sign shows decreasing velocity.

✍️ Worked example – Satellite in circular orbit

1
Identify: A satellite moves at constant distance \(6.7\times10^3\,\mathrm{km}\) from Earth’s centre. Each orbit takes 90 min. We need average speed, instantaneous velocity description, and displacement after certain times.
2
Data: \(r = 6.7\times10^6\,\mathrm{m}\), \(T = 90\times60 = 5400\,\mathrm{s}\). Circumference \(= 2\pi r\).
3
Equation: Average speed \(v = \frac{\text{circumference}}{T}\).
4
Answer: \(v = \frac{2\pi (6.7\times10^6)}{5400} = 7.8\times10^3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The instantaneous velocity has constant magnitude but direction is always tangent to the circle. After 360 min (4 orbits) displacement = 0 (back to start). After 405 min (4.5 orbits) displacement = \( -6.7\times10^3\,\mathrm{km}\) (opposite side of Earth).
Fig 6 — Satellite instantaneous velocity is tangent to the orbit; displacement measured from Earth’s centre.

🌍 Real-world: GPS and displacement

GPS devices calculate your displacement from the destination, not the distance along roads. They need vector maths (velocity and acceleration) to predict arrival times. Fighter pilots and athletes also use acceleration data to optimise performance.

✓ Examiner tip: Always state the reference point and direction when giving a displacement or velocity vector – marks are lost if direction is omitted.

🚀 HL Extension – Instantaneous acceleration as derivative

In calculus terms, \(a = \frac{dv}{dt}\) and \(v = \frac{ds}{dt}\). For non‑uniform motion, the slope of the velocity–time graph at a point gives instantaneous acceleration. Challenge: If \(v(t) = 5t^2 + 2t\), find \(a(t)\). (Answer: \(a(t) = 10t + 2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).)

MisconceptionCorrect view

"If speed is constant, velocity is constant."Velocity can change direction (e.g., circular motion) while speed stays constant → acceleration exists.
"Negative acceleration always means slowing down."Negative acceleration means velocity is becoming more negative. If velocity is also negative, the object speeds up.
"An object at rest has zero acceleration."At the top of a thrown ball, instantaneous velocity is zero but acceleration is \(g\) downward (not zero).
⚠️ Most common slip: Confusing distance with displacement in vector calculations. Always include direction (e.g., "300 km northeast") for displacement, and do not use direction for distance.
\( \text{Scalar} = \text{magnitude only} \) \( \text{Vector} = \text{magnitude + direction} \) \( \text{distance} \ge |\text{displacement}| \) \( v = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} \) \( a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} \) Instantaneous = slope of tangent

lessons.A.1__03__Graphs of Motion:
1 Lesson 1 of 4 · A.1 Kinematics
Graphs of Motion
Master displacement–time, velocity–time, and acceleration–time graphs — the visual language that unlocks every kinematics problem in IB Physics.

🎯 Hook – The crash that tells a story

During a controlled crash test, engineers don't just watch the collision — they read it from a graph. A velocity–time graph of the impact shows the car accelerating on the test track, travelling at constant speed, then in just 80 milliseconds, velocity plunging to zero. Hidden inside that graph is the displacement, the deceleration force, and the exact moment the airbag must fire. Every detail of the crash is encoded in the shape, gradient, and area of a single graph.

Fig 1 — Velocity–time graph of a crash-test vehicle. Phase A (rising): constant acceleration on the track. Phase B (flat): constant speed approach. Phase C (steep drop): violent deceleration on impact. The area of each phase = displacement for that phase.
💡 Diagnostic question (think first — answer below) — Looking at Phase C on the graph above, the line is nearly vertical (extremely steep negative gradient). What does this tell you about the acceleration during the crash? Answer: a very large negative acceleration (deceleration). Gradient = Δv/Δt — a near-vertical line means a huge change in velocity in a tiny time interval, i.e. enormous deceleration force.

📐 Displacement–time (s–t) graphs

A displacement–time graph plots position \(s\) (metres) on the vertical axis against time \(t\) (seconds) on the horizontal. It records where the object is at every moment.

The gradient of an s–t graph equals the velocity. For a straight-line segment the velocity is constant; for a curved section, draw a tangent at the point of interest — its gradient gives the instantaneous velocity (key HL skill).

Velocity from an s–t graph $$v = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \text{gradient of the } s\text{–}t \text{ graph}$$
Fig 2 — Straight line → constant velocity. Steeper = faster. Negative slope = moving in −ve direction. Horizontal = stationary (v = 0).
Fig 3 — Curved s–t graph. Steepening curve = speeding up. Flattening curve = slowing down. Horizontal end = object has stopped.
💡 Key rule: On an s–t graph the y-value tells you position; the gradient tells you velocity. A steep graph ≠ large acceleration — it means large speed. Acceleration requires a change in gradient (a curve).

📐 Velocity–time (v–t) graphs

The velocity–time graph is the most information-rich motion graph. From it you can extract both acceleration (gradient) and displacement (area).

Acceleration from a v–t graph $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \text{gradient of the } v\text{–}t \text{ graph}$$
Displacement from a v–t graph $$s = \text{area between graph line and time axis}$$

Area above the time axis = positive displacement. Area below the time axis = negative displacement (object moving in reverse). The line crossing the axis means the object momentarily has zero velocity and is reversing direction.

Fig 4 — Composite v–t graph. Rising segment (gradient = +a): acceleration. Flat segment (gradient = 0): constant velocity. Falling segment (gradient = −a): deceleration. Each shaded area = displacement for that phase. Sum all three areas for total displacement.
⚠️ Area trap: When the v–t line crosses the x-axis, split the total area at the crossing point. The area above = positive displacement; the area below = negative displacement. Adding both as positive values gives total distance, not net displacement.

📐 Acceleration–time (a–t) graphs

An acceleration–time graph plots \(a\) (m s\(^{-2}\)) against time. Its defining property: the area under the graph equals the change in velocity.

Change in velocity from an a–t graph $$\Delta v = \text{area between the } a\text{–}t \text{ graph and the time axis}$$
Fig 5 — Constant acceleration: horizontal line. Shaded area = Δv gained. If starting from rest, final velocity = area.
Fig 6 — Linked graphs for uniform acceleration: s–t parabola (blue), v–t straight line (purple). The gradient chain connects them: grad(s–t) → v–t; grad(v–t) → a–t.
✓ The gradient–area chain (HL essential): grad(s–t) = v · grad(v–t) = a · area(v–t) = s · area(a–t) = Δv. This chain underpins every kinematics calculation in IB Physics.

Fig 8 — Parabolic s–t graph for uniform acceleration from rest \((s = \frac{1}{2}at^2)\). The curve steepens because velocity increases. Tangent at any point gives instantaneous v.

✍️ Worked example – Reading a composite v–t graph

A car starts from rest. It accelerates uniformly to 24 m s⁻¹ in 6 s, travels at constant velocity for 4 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 3 s. Calculate (a) the acceleration in phase 1, (b) the deceleration in phase 3, (c) the total displacement.

1
Identify: Three-phase v–t graph. Acceleration = gradient of each phase. Displacement = area under each phase (triangles and rectangle). We need gradient of phase 1, gradient of phase 3, and sum of all three areas.
2
Data: Phase 1: \(u = 0\), \(v = 24\) m s⁻¹, \(\Delta t = 6\) s. Phase 2: \(v = 24\) m s⁻¹ (constant), \(\Delta t = 4\) s. Phase 3: \(u = 24\) m s⁻¹, \(v = 0\), \(\Delta t = 3\) s.
3
Equations and substitution:
(a) \(\;a_1 = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{24-0}{6} = +4\) m s\(^{-2}\)

(b) \(\;a_3 = \dfrac{0-24}{3} = -8\) m s\(^{-2}\) (deceleration magnitude: 8 m s\(^{-2}\))

(c) \(\;s = \tfrac{1}{2}(6)(24) + (4)(24) + \tfrac{1}{2}(3)(24) = 72 + 96 + 36 = 204\) m
4
Answer: Acceleration = \(+4\) m s\(^{-2}\); deceleration magnitude = \(8\) m s\(^{-2}\); total displacement = 204 m. The steeper phase-3 gradient (magnitude) confirms a larger deceleration — the same speed change occurs in half the time.
Fig 9 — v–t graph for the worked example. Phase 1 triangle (area = 72 m), phase 2 rectangle (area = 96 m), phase 3 triangle (area = 36 m). Total shaded area = 204 m. Note phase 3 has a steeper slope than phase 1 — larger deceleration magnitude.

🚗 Real-world: Airbag deployment timing

Airbag control units use an accelerometer to record the vehicle's deceleration as an a–t signal. The processor continuously integrates this signal (computing the area under the a–t graph) to find \(\Delta v\). When \(\Delta v\) exceeds a threshold in under 15 ms — a tiny rectangular area on the a–t graph — the airbag ignites. Engineers design for decelerations of 30–50 g over ≈ 6 ms. A v–t graph of the crash shows the velocity collapsing from ≈ 50 km h⁻¹ to zero in that 6 ms window.

✓ Examiner tip: When asked to "determine the change in velocity from an a–t graph," always state the geometric shape (rectangle, triangle, or trapezium), write out the area calculation explicitly, and include units (m s⁻¹). Each of these steps earns a mark.

🚀 HL Extension – Instantaneous values from curved graphs

At HL, v–t graphs can be curved (non-uniform acceleration). The instantaneous acceleration equals the gradient of the tangent to the curve. Similarly, displacement from a curved v–t graph is estimated by counting grid squares under the curve.

The kinematic equations \(v = u + at\), \(s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2\) etc. are valid only for uniform acceleration (straight-line v–t). For a curved v–t you must use graphical methods.

Challenge: A v–t graph is a straight line from \((0,\,0)\) to \((T,\,v_0)\). Show that the area formula gives \(s = \tfrac{1}{2}v_0 T\) and identify which kinematic equation this corresponds to. (Answer: area of triangle = \(\tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)t = \tfrac{1}{2}(0+v_0)T\) — this IS the kinematic equation \(s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u+v)t\).)

⚠️ Trap corner – common mistakes

MisconceptionCorrect view
"Steep s–t graph = large acceleration"Steep s–t gradient = large velocity. Acceleration requires a change in gradient — only a curve on the s–t graph shows acceleration.
"Gradient of v–t = displacement"Gradient of v–t = acceleration. Area under v–t = displacement. These are completely different operations.
"When v = 0, acceleration = 0"At the peak of a throw, v = 0 but a = −g ≠ 0. Velocity and acceleration are independent quantities.
"Area under v–t always = distance"Area below the x-axis counts as negative displacement. For net displacement use signed areas; for total distance take all areas as positive.
"Horizontal a–t line means object is stopped"A horizontal a–t line at a = 0 means constant velocity — the object could be moving fast. It is stopped only if v = 0 as well.
⚠️ Most common exam slip: Swapping gradient and area on a v–t graph — writing "area = acceleration" or "gradient = displacement." This single error loses marks on both Paper 1 MCQs and Paper 2 data questions. Always ask yourself: Is the question asking about the gradient or the area?
grad(s–t) = v grad(v–t) = a area(v–t) = s area(a–t) = Δv tangent → instantaneous value area below axis = −ve displacement

lessons.C.1__02__SHM Equations — Displacement, V:
2 Lesson 2 of 5 · C.1
SHM Equations: Displacement, Velocity & Acceleration
The sinusoidal solutions, phase relationships between x, v and a, and the velocity–displacement equation

Angular frequency ω

The constant ω (omega) links the defining equation a = −ω²x to the period and frequency of the motion. It tells us how rapidly the phase of the oscillation changes — one full cycle corresponds to a phase change of 2π radians.

ω = 2π / T = 2πf    (unit: rad s⁻¹)
💡 ω is not the same as frequency f. Angular frequency is measured in rad s⁻¹, while f is in Hz. They are related by ω = 2πf.

Displacement as a function of time

The solution to a = −ω²x is a sinusoidal function. The form depends on where the object starts at t = 0:

x = x₀ cos(ωt)    (starts at x = x₀ = A, i.e. extreme position)
x = x₀ sin(ωt)    (starts at x = 0, i.e. mean position)

In the IB syllabus, both forms are accepted. The key insight: displacement varies sinusoidally with time, with amplitude x₀ (= A) and angular frequency ω.

💡 The IB data booklet gives both x = x₀ sin(ωt) and x = x₀ cos(ωt). You should be comfortable using either depending on initial conditions.

Velocity as a function of time

Velocity is the time derivative of displacement. Starting from x = x₀ cos(ωt):

v = dx/dt = −ωx₀ sin(ωt)

And from x = x₀ sin(ωt):

v = dx/dt = ωx₀ cos(ωt)

The maximum speed occurs when the sine (or cosine) factor equals ±1:

v_max = ωx₀ = ωA
⚠️ Velocity leads or lags displacement by π/2 radians (a quarter cycle). When displacement is at its maximum (extreme), velocity is zero — and vice versa.

Acceleration as a function of time

Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity. Starting from v = −ωx₀ sin(ωt):

a = dv/dt = −ω²x₀ cos(ωt) = −ω²x

This confirms the defining equation a = −ω²x. The maximum acceleration magnitude is:

a_max = ω²x₀ = ω²A    (at the extremes, x = ±A)

Acceleration is in antiphase with displacement (π radians out of phase) — when displacement is maximum positive, acceleration is maximum negative.

Fig 1 — Displacement (x), velocity (v) and acceleration (a) plotted against time. Note how v leads x by π/2, and a is in antiphase (π) with x. When x is at a maximum, v = 0 and a is at its most negative.

Phase relationships — summary

Displacement x

x₀ cos(ωt) — reference phase.

Velocity v

−ωx₀ sin(ωt) — leads x by π/2.

Acceleration a

−ω²x₀ cos(ωt) — in antiphase with x (π rad out of phase). Leads v by π/2.

v leads x by π/2 a is π out of phase with x a leads v by π/2 v_max = ωA a_max = ω²A

Velocity as a function of displacement

A critical equation that bypasses time entirely. Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1:

v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²)

This tells us the speed at any displacement x. Key deductions:

PositionxSpeed |v|
Mean position0ωx₀ (maximum)
Extremes±A0
HalfwayA/2ω√(3/4)·A ≈ 0.866 ωA
⚠️ The ± sign indicates the object passes through most positions twice per cycle — once going one way, once returning. The speed is the same, but velocity direction differs.
Fig 2 — The velocity–displacement relationship traces an ellipse. At x = 0 the speed is maximum (ωA); at x = ±A the speed is zero. The ± indicates two directions of travel through each point.

Worked Example — Finding v_max, a_max and speed at a given displacement

A particle oscillates in SHM with amplitude 0.040 m and frequency 3.0 Hz.

1
Find ω: ω = 2πf = 2π × 3.0 = 18.85 rad s⁻¹
2
Maximum speed: v_max = ωA = 18.85 × 0.040 = 0.754 m s⁻¹
3
Maximum acceleration: a_max = ω²A = (18.85)² × 0.040 = 14.2 m s⁻²
4
Speed at x = 0.030 m: v = ω√(A² − x²) = 18.85 × √(0.0016 − 0.0009) = 18.85 × 0.02646 = 0.499 m s⁻¹
✓ Always show your substitution step clearly — examiners award marks for correct substitution even if the final numerical answer is wrong.

Energy in SHM
Kinetic energy, potential energy, total energy, and their variation with displacement and time

Energy overview

In SHM, energy continuously interchanges between kinetic (KE) and potential (PE) forms, while the total mechanical energy remains constant (assuming no damping).

The velocity of an object in SHM varies with displacement as:

v² = ω²(A² − x²)   ⟹   vmax = ωA (at x = 0)

From this, kinetic energy is:

KE = ½mv² = ½mω²(A² − x²)

Potential energy (stored in whichever store provides the restoring force):

PE = ½mω²x²

Total energy (constant, independent of x):

Etotal = ½mω²A²
Fig 1 — Energy vs displacement for SHM. KE is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A. PE is the reverse. Total energy is constant.

Key energy relationships

PositionxKEPESpeedAcceleration
Mean position0MaximumZeroMaximum (= ωA)Zero
Extreme (±A)±AZeroMaximumZeroMaximum (= ω²A)
Any position xx½mω²(A²−x²)½mω²x²ω√(A²−x²)ω²x
Total energy E = ½mω²A² = ½kA² (for a spring). Total energy is proportional to A² — doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy.

Energy as a function of time

If x = A cos(ωt), then:

KE = ½mω²A² sin²(ωt)     PE = ½mω²A² cos²(ωt)

Both KE and PE oscillate at twice the frequency of the displacement — they complete two full cycles per period T. This is because energy depends on the square of displacement or velocity.

At every instant: KE + PE = ½mω²A² = constant.

Where does KE = PE?

Setting KE = PE:

½mω²(A² − x²) = ½mω²x²  ⟹  A² = 2x²  ⟹  x = ±A/√2

At x = ±A/√2, the energy is equally split. Each form carries exactly half the total: KE = PE = ¼mω²A².

KE = PE at x = A/√2 E ∝ A² E ∝ ω² KE + PE = constant

The Simple Pendulum & Mass–Spring System
Deriving the period equations, conditions for SHM, and comparing the two key systems

System 1 — Mass on a spring

Conditions: spring mass negligible, Hooke's law obeyed (spring constant k), air friction negligible, g constant, fixed support.

When displaced x from equilibrium, the restoring force is F = −kx. Applying Newton's second law: ma = −kx, so a = −(k/m)x.

Comparing with a = −ω²x gives:

ω² = k/m   ⟹   T = 2π√(m/k)

T increases with greater mass m (heavier → slower) and decreases with stiffer spring k (stiffer → faster).

The period T of a mass–spring system does NOT depend on amplitude (isochronous) or on gravitational field strength g. It works identically on Earth, the Moon, or in space.
Fig 1 — Mass on a spring. When displaced x from equilibrium, F = −kx always points back towards the mean position.

System 2 — Simple pendulum

Conditions: string mass negligible, air friction negligible, angle of swing < 5° (0.1 rad), g constant, fixed pivot, string length l constant.

The restoring force is the component of gravity along the arc: F = −mg sinθ. For small angles, sinθ ≈ θ = x/l, so F ≈ −mg(x/l) = −(mg/l)x.

This gives a = −(g/l)x, hence:

ω² = g/l   ⟹   T = 2π√(l/g)
The mass of the bob does NOT appear in the formula — it cancels in the derivation. T depends only on l and g.
Fig 2 — Simple pendulum. For small angles, mg sinθ ≈ mgθ, making the restoring force proportional to displacement.
A pendulum released from 30° does NOT undergo SHM. At large angles sinθ ≠ θ, so F is not proportional to x. SHM is only a valid approximation for θ < 5°.

Mass–spring

T = 2π√(m/k)

T ∝ √m (heavier → longer T)
T ∝ 1/√k (stiffer → shorter T)
Independent of g
Works in any orientation

Simple pendulum

T = 2π√(l/g)

T ∝ √l (longer → longer T)
T ∝ 1/√g (stronger g → shorter T)
Independent of mass m
Requires small angle (< 5°)
Both are isochronous (T independent of A) Spring: T depends on m and k Pendulum: T depends on l and g

T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(0.6/30) = 2π√(0.02) = 0.889 s
f = 1/T = 1/0.889 ≈ 1.1 Hz

5 Lesson 5 of 5 · IB DP Physics
Damping & Resonance
Damped oscillations, forced oscillations, natural frequency, and the resonance phenomenon

What is damping?

Damping is the progressive loss of energy from an oscillating system due to resistive forces (friction, air resistance, viscous drag). The amplitude gradually decreases over time, and the oscillation eventually ceases.

In a damped system, total mechanical energy is no longer conserved — it is dissipated as thermal energy (heat) in the surroundings.

Damping reduces the amplitude of oscillation but does NOT significantly change the frequency (for light damping). The system still oscillates near its natural frequency.

Three regimes of damping

Underdamped

Amplitude decreases gradually over many cycles.

The system oscillates with an exponentially decaying envelope.

Example: a pendulum in air.

Critically damped

System returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating.

No overshoot past equilibrium.

Example: car shock absorbers.

Overdamped

System returns to equilibrium slowly without oscillating.

Takes longer than critical damping.

Example: door closer mechanism.
Underdamped: oscillates, amplitude decays Critical: fastest return, no oscillation Overdamped: slow return, no oscillation
Fig 1 — The three regimes of damping. Underdamped: amplitude decays exponentially over many cycles. Critically damped: fastest return to equilibrium without overshoot. Overdamped: slow return, no oscillation.
In IB exams, you should be able to sketch all three damping curves on the same displacement–time graph. Underdamped shows decaying sinusoidal oscillation; critically damped shows the fastest smooth return to zero; overdamped shows an even slower return.

Natural frequency

Every oscillating system has a natural frequency f₀ — the frequency at which it oscillates freely when displaced and released with no driving force and no damping.

f₀ = 1/(2π) × √(k/m)    (mass-spring)     f₀ = 1/(2π) × √(g/l)    (pendulum)

The natural frequency is determined only by the physical properties of the system (mass, spring constant, length, etc.), not by how it is driven or damped.

Forced oscillations

A forced oscillation occurs when an external periodic force is applied to a system. The system is driven at a driving frequency fd which may differ from its natural frequency f₀.

After initial transients die away, the system oscillates at the driving frequency fd, not its natural frequency. The amplitude of the steady-state oscillation depends on how close fd is to f₀.

Resonance

Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system:

fd = f₀   ⟹   Resonance (maximum amplitude)

At resonance, energy transfer from driver to oscillator is most efficient. The amplitude reaches a maximum, limited only by damping. In the absence of damping, the amplitude would theoretically grow without bound.

At resonance, the driving force is exactly π/2 radians (90°) out of phase with the displacement. This means the force is always in the direction of the velocity, maximizing power transfer.

The resonance curve

A graph of amplitude vs driving frequency shows a characteristic resonance peak:

FeatureLight dampingHeavy damping
Peak amplitudeTall and sharpLow and broad
Peak frequencyVery close to f₀Slightly below f₀
BandwidthNarrowWide
Q factorHighLow

As damping increases, the resonance peak becomes broader and lower, and the peak shifts slightly below f₀. With very heavy damping, resonance effectively disappears.

Light damping → sharp peak Heavy damping → broad, low peak No damping → infinite amplitude (theory)

Phase relationship in forced oscillations

ConditionPhase difference (driver vs displacement)
fd ≪ f₀≈ 0 (in phase — system follows the driver)
fd = f₀ (resonance)π/2 (90° — driver leads displacement by quarter cycle)
fd ≫ f₀≈ π (antiphase — system opposes the driver)
The phase changes most rapidly near resonance. This smooth transition from 0 to π (through π/2 at resonance) is a key feature of the IB syllabus.

Real-world examples

SystemResonance exampleUseful or harmful?
Tuning forkVibrates strongly at its natural frequency when struckUseful (musical)
Radio receiverElectrical circuit tuned to match broadcast frequencyUseful
Microwave ovenMicrowaves at the natural frequency of water moleculesUseful
Bridge / buildingWind or earthquake frequency matches structural f₀Harmful (Tacoma Narrows)
Wine glassSound at glass's natural frequency causes shatteringDemonstration

lessons.C.2__01__Wave Properties — Amplitude, Fr:
IB Diploma ProgrammeTheme C: Wave BehaviourSL & HL

C.2.01 — Wave Properties

Amplitude, Frequency, Wavelength, Period, Phase Difference & Graphical Representations
Syllabus Content: Wavelength \(\lambda\), frequency \(f\), time period \(T\), and wave speed \(v\), applied to wave motion as given by \( v = f\lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T} \). Displacement–distance and displacement–time graphs.

1. What Is a Wave?

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another. For mechanical waves, this happens through oscillations of particles in a medium. For electromagnetic waves, it happens through oscillating electric and magnetic fields. The crucial principle:

Key Principle
Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. The particles of the medium oscillate about their equilibrium positions but do not travel with the wave. Only the pattern — and the energy — propagates.

Consider shaking one end of a taut rope up and down continuously. A pattern of crests and troughs propagates along the rope. Each segment simply moves up and down — what travels is the disturbance and, with it, energy and momentum.

Ref: Cambridge Fig 13.1 / Hodder Fig C2.2

If the motion of the hand is continuous and periodic, a continuous travelling wave is established. If it is a single brief disturbance, we get a wave pulse.

How Does a Wave Transfer Energy?

As the wave travels, particles of the medium perform simple harmonic oscillations (SHM) about their equilibrium positions. From Topic C.1, we know that SHM involves kinetic and elastic potential energy. This energy is supplied by the source. In each period the source provides energy \(E\) to produce one full wave. As the wave progresses, this energy flows through the medium in the direction of propagation. The speed of energy transfer equals the wave speed.

2. Fundamental Wave Quantities

Wavelength (\(\lambda\))

The wavelength is the shortest distance between two points on the wave that are in phase — for instance, from crest to crest, or trough to trough. More precisely:

Definition — Wavelength
The wavelength \(\lambda\) is the shortest distance between two points moving in phase on a wave. SI unit: metre (m).

Amplitude (\(A\) or \(x_0\))

The amplitude is the maximum displacement of any particle from its equilibrium (rest) position. It is always positive.

Exam Tip — Common Mistake
The amplitude is NOT the crest-to-trough distance! That distance is twice the amplitude. The amplitude is measured from the equilibrium line to the crest (or to the trough). This is one of the most frequent errors in IB exams.

Time Period (\(T\))

Definition — Time Period
The period \(T\) is the time for one complete oscillation of a particle within the medium, or the time for one complete wave to pass a fixed point. SI unit: second (s).

Frequency (\(f\))

Definition — Frequency
The frequency \(f\) is the number of complete oscillations per second, or the number of complete wavelengths passing a fixed point per second. SI unit: hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹.
Frequency–Period Relationship
\[ \boxed{\; f \;=\; \dfrac{1}{T} \;} \]
\(f\) in Hz, \(T\) in seconds. If \(T = 0.25\) s, then \(f = 4\) Hz.

Summary of Quantities

Wavelength \(\lambda\)Shortest distance between two in-phase points (m) Amplitude \(A\)Maximum displacement from equilibrium (m) Period \(T\)Time for one complete oscillation (s) Frequency \(f\)Oscillations per second (Hz) CrestPoint of maximum positive displacement TroughPoint of maximum negative displacement

3. Graphical Representations of Waves

Two types of graph are used to represent waves. They look similar (both sinusoidal) but convey different information.

Displacement–Distance Graph (Snapshot)

This is like a photograph of the entire wave at one specific moment in time. The horizontal axis is position (distance along the wave) and the vertical axis is displacement.

What you can read from it:

  • The amplitude — maximum displacement
  • The wavelength — distance between adjacent crests (or troughs)

What you CANNOT directly read: the period or frequency (these require time information).

Displacement–Time Graph (Video of One Point)

This is like a video focused on one specific point in the medium, recording how its displacement changes over time. The horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is displacement.

What you can read from it:

  • The amplitude
  • The period — time between adjacent crests

What you CANNOT directly read: the wavelength (this requires spatial information).

Exam Tip — Reading Periods Accurately
To find the period, count several full cycles and divide. For example, if 3 complete periods span 10 ms, then \(T = 10/3 = 3.33\) ms. This reduces reading error. Also always check the units on the time axis — they may be ms, μs, or s!
Exam Tip — Transverse or Longitudinal?
You cannot tell whether a wave is transverse or longitudinal from a displacement–distance or displacement–time graph alone. Both produce sinusoidal shapes. The graphs look identical for both types — the direction of displacement is not shown by the graph shape.

Connecting the Two Graphs

If you know both graphs for the same wave, you can determine the wave speed:

  • Read \(\lambda\) from the displacement–distance graph
  • Read \(T\) from the displacement–time graph
  • Calculate \(v = \lambda / T\)
Worked Example 1 — Reading Both Graphs
A displacement–distance graph gives \(\lambda = 0.40\) m and a displacement–time graph for the same wave gives \(T = 3.33\) ms. Find the frequency and the wave speed.
Solution

Frequency:

\[ f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{3.33 \times 10^{-3}} = 300 \text{ Hz} \]

Wave speed:

\[ v = f\lambda = 300 \times 0.40 = 120 \text{ m s}^{-1} \]

4. Phase Difference

When we compare two waves (or two points on the same wave), the phase difference describes how "out of step" they are. It is measured in radians (or degrees).

Phase Difference Between Two Points
\[ \boxed{\; \Delta\phi \;=\; 2\pi\,\frac{\Delta x}{\lambda} \;} \]
\(\Delta x\) = distance between the two points; \(\lambda\) = wavelength. Also equivalent: \(\Delta\phi = 2\pi\,\frac{\Delta t}{T}\)

Important Special Cases

\(\Delta x = 0\)\(\Delta\phi = 0\) — the points are in phase \(\Delta x = \lambda/4\)\(\Delta\phi = \pi/2\) — quarter-wave phase difference \(\Delta x = \lambda/2\)\(\Delta\phi = \pi\) — the points are in anti-phase (180° out) \(\Delta x = \lambda\)\(\Delta\phi = 2\pi\) — equivalent to being in phase again
Critical Thinking — Phase and Full Wavelengths

Two points on a wave are separated by 1.5 wavelengths. What is their phase difference?

\(\Delta\phi = 2\pi \times 1.5 = 3\pi\) rad. Since phase difference is cyclic (mod \(2\pi\)), we get \(3\pi - 2\pi = \pi\). So the points are in anti-phase, not in phase! Always reduce phase differences modulo \(2\pi\).

Critical Thinking — Which Direction Is the Wave Travelling?

Given a displacement–distance graph at \(t = 0\) and a displacement–time graph of a specific point, you can determine the wave's direction. At \(t = 0\), read the position of the point on the distance graph. Check from the time graph which way the displacement changes just after \(t = 0\). Then mentally shift the wave pattern left or right on the distance graph to see which shift produces that change. This is a frequently examined higher-order skill.

IB Diploma ProgrammeTheme CSL & HL

C.2.02 — Transverse & Longitudinal Waves

Wave types, particle motion, sound waves, compressions & rarefactions, and mechanical vs electromagnetic waves
Syllabus Content: Transverse and longitudinal travelling waves. The nature of sound waves. The differences between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves.

1. Transverse Waves

Definition — Transverse Wave
A wave is transverse if the displacement of the particles of the medium is at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction of energy transfer.

In a transverse wave on a rope, the rope segments oscillate up and down while the wave pattern propagates horizontally. The highest points are crests and the lowest are troughs. Each particle performs SHM with the same frequency as the wave but is slightly out of phase with its neighbour.

Examples: waves on strings, ropes, and water surfaces; all electromagnetic waves; seismic S-waves.

Determining Particle Motion from a Snapshot

This is a key exam skill. Given the wave direction and a displacement–distance graph, you can find which way any particle will move next:

  1. Draw the wave profile (solid line) at the current instant.
  2. Draw a copy of the wave (dashed line) shifted slightly in the direction of propagation.
  3. Each particle moves vertically from its position on the solid curve towards its position on the dashed curve.
Exam Tip — Velocity at Crests and Equilibrium
At a crest or trough: the particle has zero velocity (momentarily at rest) but maximum acceleration (directed towards equilibrium). At the equilibrium position: the particle has maximum speed but zero acceleration. This follows directly from SHM.

2. Longitudinal Waves

Definition — Longitudinal Wave
A wave is longitudinal if the displacement of the particles is parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal waves consist of alternating compressions and rarefactions.

Imagine pushing and pulling one end of a slinky spring along its length. Coils crowd together (compression) and then spread apart (rarefaction). These regions propagate along the spring.

[IMAGE C2-04] — Longitudinal wave on a slinky showing compressions (coils bunched) and
CompressionA region where particles are closer together than at equilibrium → higher density and pressure. RarefactionA region where particles are further apart than at equilibrium → lower density and pressure.

Displacement–Distance Graphs for Longitudinal Waves

We represent longitudinal waves using the same sinusoidal graph style. The key difference: the displacement axis represents particle displacement along the wave direction. Positive displacement = motion in the direction of wave travel; negative = opposite.

Locating Compressions and Rarefactions on the Graph

This is one of the most commonly tested and most commonly wrong topics:

  • A compression occurs where displacement is zero and the gradient is negative (for a wave moving right). Particles on the left have moved right and particles on the right have moved left — they've crowded together.
  • A rarefaction occurs where displacement is zero and the gradient is positive. Particles on both sides have moved away from this point.
Exam Tip — Critical Error to Avoid
Compressions and rarefactions are NOT at the peaks and troughs of the displacement graph. They occur at the zero-crossing points. This is the single most common error with longitudinal wave graphs. At the peaks/troughs, the displacement is maximum but the density is approximately normal (equilibrium separation).
Worked Example 1 — Longitudinal Wave Analysis
A longitudinal wave travels to the right. A displacement–distance graph shows that at point P (at x = 20 cm), the displacement is zero and the graph is transitioning from positive to negative. Is P a compression or rarefaction?
Solution

At P, the gradient is negative. Particles to the left of P have positive displacement (moved right, towards P). Particles to the right of P have negative displacement (moved left, towards P). Particles on both sides have moved towards P → higher density → P is a compression.

3. Sound Waves

Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave. It is produced when a vibrating surface (loudspeaker, vocal cord, tuning fork) creates alternating compressions and rarefactions in the surrounding air.

Key Facts About Sound

  • Medium required: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
  • Typical speed in air: ~340 m s⁻¹ at room temperature (increases slightly with temperature).
  • Speed in different media: Generally fastest in solids, slowest in gases — because particles are closer and inter-particle forces are stronger in solids.
  • Audible range: approximately 20 Hz – 20 kHz.
  • Pitch: determined by frequency (higher f → higher pitch).
  • Loudness: determined by amplitude (greater A → louder).

To give a sense of scale: at the threshold of hearing (1000 Hz), the pressure variation at the eardrum exceeds atmospheric by just 20 μPa (atmospheric pressure is ~10⁵ Pa). The corresponding molecular displacement is about 10⁻¹¹ m — a tenth of a hydrogen atom's diameter!

4. Mechanical vs Electromagnetic Waves

PropertyMechanical WavesElectromagnetic Waves
Requires medium?Yes — solid, liquid, or gasNo — can travel through vacuum
What oscillates?Particles of the medium (masses)Electric and magnetic fields
TypeCan be transverse or longitudinalAlways transverse
Speed in vacuumCannot exist in vacuum\(c = 3.00 \times 10^8\) m s⁻¹
Speed depends on…Medium properties (density, stiffness)Same for all EM waves in vacuum; varies slightly in materials
ExamplesSound, water waves, seismic wavesLight, radio, X-rays, microwaves, gamma rays
Critical Thinking — Why Can't Transverse Waves Travel Through Gases?

Transverse mechanical waves require a restoring force perpendicular to the direction of propagation. This requires the medium to sustain shear stress. Gases (and bulk liquids) have no fixed molecular structure and cannot resist shear — their molecules simply slide past each other. Hence only longitudinal (compression) waves can propagate. This explains why seismic S-waves (transverse) cannot pass through Earth's liquid outer core, while P-waves (longitudinal) can — giving evidence for the core's liquid state.

Critical Thinking — Water Surface Waves: Truly Transverse?

We often call water surface waves "transverse," but this is a simplification. In deep water, individual water particles actually move in circles (or ellipses in shallow water) — combining both vertical and horizontal motion. The surface appears to move transversely, but the underlying particle motion is more complex. This is a good example of how models simplify reality.

5. Exam-Style Questions

Q is at a zero crossing with negative gradient. R is at maximum positive displacement. S is at a zero crossing with positive gradient.
(a) State the amplitude of the wave. [1]
(b) State which particle is at the centre of a compression. Explain. [2]

Wave Speed, Sound & Light
Understanding wave graphs, the speed of mechanical waves, properties of sound, and the electromagnetic nature of light.

📊 Displacement–time graphs for any wave

A displacement–time graph shows the oscillation of a single particle in the medium as the wave passes. The vertical axis represents displacement (either parallel or perpendicular to wave travel), so the same graph shape works for both transverse and longitudinal waves. A common mistake is to think it only shows a transverse wave — but the direction is not specified in the graph.

Fig C2.9 — Displacement‑time graph. The period T is the time for one complete cycle.
💡 The wave’s frequency f = 1/T. For a wave of frequency 4.0 Hz, the period T = 0.25 s. Sketching such a graph requires marking the amplitude (2.0 cm) and the period correctly.

🌊 Wave pulses

A wave pulse is a single short‑duration disturbance. For example, touching a water surface once with a fingertip produces an expanding circular pulse.

Fig C2.10 — A wave pulse (single oscillation).
Fig C2.11 — Longitudinal wave. Compressions (high density) and rarefactions (low density).

In a longitudinal wave (e.g. sound), particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Regions of high pressure are compressions; low pressure are rarefactions.

🔊 Sound waves – nature and speed

Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave requiring a medium. It cannot travel in a vacuum. The speed depends on:

  • How close the particles are (density)
  • Strength of interparticle forces
Fig C2.12 — Air molecules form compressions and rarefactions as sound passes.
v = f λ  where v = wave speed (m s⁻¹), f = frequency (Hz), λ = wavelength (m)
⚠️ The displacement‑time graph for a sound wave can also be drawn as a pressure‑time graph (variations above and below atmospheric pressure).

Worked example — wavelength of sound (C2.2)

1

2
Use v = fλ → λ = v / f.
3

4

✓ For a wave in steel with same frequency and λ = 26.1 m, v = fλ = 196 × 26.1 = 5120 m s⁻¹. The speed is greater because particles are closer together and forces are stronger.

🎵 Pitch, loudness and decibels

Fig C2.14 — Higher frequency → higher pitch.
Fig C2.15 — Larger amplitude → louder sound.

Pitch is related to frequency; loudness is related to amplitude (intensity). The human ear detects intensities over an enormous range, so we use a logarithmic decibel (dB) scale.

Fig C2.16 — Approximate sound levels in decibels. +10 dB = 10× more intense.
💡 On a log scale, equal increments represent multiplication by the same factor. For sound: β (dB) = 10 log₁₀(I / I₀).

💡 Light as an electromagnetic wave

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave that does not require a medium. It consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel.

Fig C2.19 — Light is a transverse EM wave.
Fig C2.20 — Visible spectrum (red: ~700 nm, violet: ~400 nm).

In a vacuum, light travels at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. In a transparent medium, speed reduces but frequency stays constant, so wavelength shortens.

c = f λ  (λmedium = vmedium / f)

Worked example — light in air and glass (C2.3)

2

4
Conclusion: Frequency unchanged, wavelength decreases when light slows down.

🔬 Sonar — using ultrasound pulses

Fig C2.18 — Pulse of ultrasound reflects from seabed; time delay gives depth.
Depth = v × (Δt / 2)  (v = speed of sound in water)

lessons.C.2__04__Intensity and Amplitude:
5 Lesson 5 of 10 · C.3 Wave Phenomena
Intensity and Amplitude of Waves
From energy concepts to the I ∝ A² relationship — build intuition, read graphs, and conquer exam‑style questions.

Why does turning up the volume feel so much louder?

A tiny ripple carries almost no energy; a tsunami can destroy coastlines. A whisper is barely audible; a rock concert can shake your chest. The difference is not just in how high the wave is (its amplitude), but in how much energy it delivers per second per square metre — its intensity.

Fig 1 — Everyday extremes: from a tiny ripple to a giant wave. The amplitude increase means far greater energy.

1. Amplitude — a quick recap

Amplitude (A) is the maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position. For a sound wave it can be measured as pressure variation; for an electromagnetic wave it’s the maximum electric field strength.

Fig 2 — A sinusoidal wave. The amplitude A is the distance from the rest position to a crest (or trough).

2. What is intensity?

Intensity (I) is the power transmitted per unit area, measured in watts per square metre (W m⁻²).

I = P / A

Imagine a light bulb radiating energy. The same total power is spread over an ever‑larger spherical surface as you move away. That’s why a star looks dim from Earth — not because it emits less power, but because the intensity is tiny when the light reaches us.

Fig 3 — For a point source, power P is spread over a sphere of area 4πr², so I = P / (4πr²). Intensity drops with the inverse‑square of distance.

3. Energy in a wave and the I ∝ A² law

The energy carried by a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude. For a sinusoidal mechanical wave, the intensity can be derived as:

I = 2π² ρ v f² A²

where ρ is the density of the medium, v the wave speed, f the frequency. For a given medium and frequency, intensity is directly proportional to amplitude squared:

I ∝ A²
💡 Examiner insight: You’ll rarely need the full constant. Most IB questions expect you to use the proportionality I₁/I₂ = (A₁/A₂)² — this works for any wave type (sound, water, light) when only amplitude changes.
⚠️ Common mistake: “If intensity doubles, amplitude doubles.” No — because of the square root: √2 ≈ 1.41. Doubling I only multiplies amplitude by about 1.4.
✓ Exam tip: Always write I₁/I₂ = (A₁/A₂)² before plugging numbers. It avoids confusion and shows the examiner you understand the proportionality.

4. Reading the relationship from graphs

The square‑law is best understood by looking at different graphs.

Fig 4 — I vs A: a parabolic curve through the origin, because I ∝ A².
Fig 5 — log I vs log A: a straight line of gradient exactly 2, confirming the square relationship.

To make the relationship linear, plot I vs A² — a straight line through the origin. The slope gives the constant 2π²ρv f².

I vs A² → straight line log I vs log A → gradient = 2

5. Inverse‑square law for a point source

When waves spread spherically from a source, amplitude also decreases with distance. Because I ∝ 1/r² and I ∝ A², it follows that A ∝ 1/r.

Fig 6 — Intensity vs distance from a point source: the rapid fall‑off follows 1/r². Amplitude would fall as 1/r.
💡 Extension (HL): The fact that A ∝ 1/r for a spherical wave comes directly from energy conservation: power through any spherical shell is constant, so 4πr₁² I₁ = 4πr₂² I₂ ⇒ I ∝ 1/r² ⇒ A ∝ 1/r.

Worked Example — Comparing two waves

Fig 7 — Wave P (top) and Wave Q (bottom). Both have the same frequency and travel in the same medium.

Wave P has amplitude X₀, Wave Q has amplitude 2X₀. They travel in the same medium with identical frequency. Find the ratio of their intensities, I_Q / I_P.

1
State the known values: A_Q = 2 X₀, A_P = X₀. Frequency and medium are identical, so the constant 2π²ρv f² cancels.
2
Write the proportional equation: I ∝ A² ⇒ I_Q / I_P = (A_Q / A_P)².
3
Substitute: I_Q / I_P = (2 X₀ / X₀)² = 2² = 4.
4
State the answer: Wave Q has 4 times the intensity of Wave P. Doubling amplitude quadruples intensity.

lessons.C.2__05__The Electromagnetic Spectrum:
5 Lesson 5 of 12 · C.2.05
The Electromagnetic Spectrum
From radio to gamma rays: wave properties, photon energy, and how to master graphs for IB Physics SL

📡 What is the electromagnetic spectrum?

The electromagnetic (EM) spectrum is the continuous range of all possible frequencies of electromagnetic radiation. It spans from very long wavelength radio waves (km scale) to extremely short gamma rays (smaller than an atomic nucleus).

All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum: c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. They differ only in frequency (f) and wavelength (λ) – and therefore in the energy they carry.

Fig 1 — The electromagnetic spectrum. Note the inverse relationship: long wavelength ↔ low frequency ↔ low energy (left) and short wavelength ↔ high frequency ↔ high energy (right).
💡 Examiner insight: You must be able to order any set of EM radiations by frequency (or wavelength). Mnemonic: Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-ray, Gamma – “Rabbits Mate In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens”.

⚡ How are EM waves created?

An oscillating electric charge (for example, electrons moving up and down in an antenna) produces a changing electric field, which in turn generates a changing magnetic field. These two fields regenerate each other and propagate outward as a transverse wave – no medium required.

Fig 2 — Propagation of an EM wave. The electric field (blue) and magnetic field (red) oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel.

📐 The wave equation – linking f and λ

For any EM wave in a vacuum, the speed \(c\) is constant. Therefore frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional:

c = f λ ⇒ f = c / λ  and  λ = c / f

If frequency doubles, wavelength halves – and vice versa.

c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s f ∝ 1/λ λ ∝ 1/f
⚠️ Common mistake: Thinking that different EM waves travel at different speeds in vacuum. They all travel at \(c\). Speed only changes in a medium (e.g., glass, water).

🔋 Photon model – quantised energy

EM waves carry energy in discrete packets called photons. The energy of a single photon depends only on its frequency (not on its intensity):

E = h f

where \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J·s}\) (Planck’s constant). Using the wave equation, we also get:

E = h c / λ

A very useful shortcut for the IB data booklet: \(hc = 1240 \text{ eV·nm}\). That means if λ is in nanometres, \(E (\text{eV}) = 1240 / \lambda (\text{nm})\).

✓ Exam tip: You will often be asked to convert between joules and electronvolts. Remember 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

📈 Graphical mastery for IB exams

Two essential graphs appear frequently in Papers 1, 2 and 3:

Fig 3 — Photon energy vs. frequency: straight line through origin, slope = h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s. Higher frequency = higher photon energy.
Fig 4 — Left: E ∝ 1/λ (hyperbola). Right: linearised plot E vs. 1/λ gives a straight line with slope = hc.

What examiners ask: Identify the slope, calculate h or hc from a graph, predict the energy for a given frequency, or determine which region of the spectrum a data point belongs to.

🔧 Worked example – calculating wavelength and photon energy

1
State the known values: A microwave oven operates at f = 2.45 GHz. \(c = 3.00\times10^8 \text{ m/s}\), \(h = 6.63\times10^{-34} \text{ J·s}\).
2
Find the wavelength: Convert GHz → Hz: 2.45 GHz = 2.45×10⁹ Hz. Use λ = c / f = (3.00×10⁸) / (2.45×10⁹) = 0.122 m.
3
Find photon energy in joules: E = h f = (6.63×10⁻³⁴)(2.45×10⁹) = 1.62×10⁻²⁴ J.
4
Convert to eV: E = (1.62×10⁻²⁴) / (1.60×10⁻¹⁹) = 1.01×10⁻⁵ eV (very low energy – non‑ionising).
💡 Examiner note: Always include units and show conversion steps. Marks are often awarded for the correct use of scientific notation.

🌍 Real‑world connections

Fig 5 — Applications across the spectrum: X‑rays (medical imaging), microwaves (cooking & radar), infrared (thermal cameras), radio (astronomy & communication).

Each region interacts with matter differently because of photon energy: radio waves pass through walls, UV causes sunburn (ionisation starts near 3.1 eV), and gamma rays sterilise medical equipment.

3 Lesson 3 of 12 · C.1 Wave Phenomena
Principle of Superposition
When two waves meet, they add together – then continue unchanged. This simple rule explains interference, standing waves, and even noise‑cancelling headphones.

🎯 Hook – The Slinky® surprise

Watch two pulses on a Slinky® approach each other. When they meet, the rope briefly shows a much larger bump – then each pulse continues as if nothing happened. They don’t bounce or destroy each other; they simply add.

Fig B — Two identical pulses pass through each other. At the moment of overlap (middle), the resultant displacement is the sum of the two.
💡 Diagnostic question (think – then click) — What does the rope look like when a positive peak meets a negative trough of the same size? (Answer: flat line – perfect cancellation, but only at that instant.)

📐 The Principle of Superposition

When two or more waves overlap at the same point in space and time, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements.

sresultant = s1 + s2 + ... + sn

Constructive interference – waves ‘in step’ (phase difference 0°, 360°, …). Peaks align → AR = A1 + A2 (bigger wave).
Destructive interference – waves ‘out of step’ (phase difference 180°, 540°, …). Peak meets trough → AR = |A1 – A2| (smaller wave).

lessons.C.3__02__Constructive and Destructive In:
4 Lesson 4 of 12 · C.3 Wave Phenomena
Single‑Slit Diffraction
How light spreads after passing through a narrow opening – interference of Huygens wavelets

🎵 Everyday phenomenon – sound & radio waves

Stand near a tall building and listen to a street musician around the corner – you hear the music clearly because sound waves diffract (spread) around obstacles. Long‑wave radio signals reach valleys behind mountains, but short‑wave TV signals cannot – diffraction is strongest when the obstacle/gap size is comparable to the wavelength.

Fig 1 – Water waves fan out into a semicircle after passing through a narrow gap. The narrower the gap, the stronger the diffraction.

⚡ Diagnostic quick‑check

B The extra distance one wave travels relative to another ✓

Foundation – Interference & Huygens

📐 Key definitions

Coherence: two sources emit waves with same frequency and constant phase difference.
Path difference: difference in distance from a point to two sources.
Constructive interference: path difference = nλ → waves in phase → bright fringe.
Destructive interference: path difference = (n+½)λ → waves out of phase → dark fringe.

💡 The principle of superposition: resultant displacement = vector sum of individual displacements.
Fig 2 – Two‑source interference in a ripple tank. Nodal lines (dark) occur where path difference = (n+½)λ.
Fig 3 – Huygens’ principle: every point across the slit acts as a wavelet source. Their superposition creates the diffraction pattern.

🔬 Introducing single‑slit diffraction

When light passes through a very narrow slit, it does not travel in a straight line but spreads out. According to Huygens, every point across the slit emits wavelets that interfere. The result is a pattern of a very bright central maximum flanked by dimmer secondary maxima, separated by completely dark minima.

Fig 4 – Actual laser pattern: bright central band, weaker side lobes.
Fig 5 – Intensity vs position on screen. Central maximum is twice as wide as side lobes and >20× brighter than first side peak.

❓ Why minima occur – pairing wavelets

For the first dark fringe at angle θ₁, take wavelets from the top edge and the midpoint of the slit. If their path difference is λ/2, they cancel. Geometry: (b/2) sinθ₁ = λ/2 → sinθ₁ = λ/b. Extending to the whole slit gives the general condition for minima:

b sinθ = nλ  (n = 1, 2, 3, …)
Fig 6 – Deriving the first minimum: path difference between top and middle ray = λ/2.
✓ For small angles: θ ≈ λ/b (in radians). Central maximum angular width = 2λ/b.
The master formula

🔑 Single‑slit minima condition

\boxed{b \sin\theta_n = n\lambda} \quad (n = 1,2,3,\dots)

Linear width of central maximum on a screen: \( w = \frac{2\lambda D}{b} \) (for small angles).
Proportionalities: θ₁ ∝ λ and θ₁ ∝ 1/b. Narrower slit → wider pattern. Longer λ → wider pattern.

lessons.C.3__03__Young's Double-Slit Experiment:
3 Lesson 3 · C.3
Young's Double-Slit Experiment
How two slits, one wavelength, and a screen reveal the wave nature of light — deriving and applying s = λD / d

Why Should You Care?

Have you ever noticed the rainbow colours on a soap bubble or a thin oil film on a puddle? Those colours come from interference — the same wave behaviour that Thomas Young used in 1801 to prove that light is a wave. When two sets of waves overlap, they can reinforce or cancel each other, creating striking patterns of bright and dark bands called fringes.

Fig 1 — Thin-film interference in everyday life. The same principle — superposition of waves with different path lengths — underlies Young's experiment.
Key definitions

Terms You Must Know

TermDefinitionSymbolUnit
CoherenceA constant phase difference between two waves (same frequency, same waveform)——
Path differenceThe extra distance one wave travels compared to the other to reach the same pointΔm
Fringe spacingDistance between the centres of adjacent bright fringessm
Slit separationCentre-to-centre distance between the two slitsdm
Screen distanceDistance from the double slit to the observation screenDm
WavelengthDistance between consecutive identical points on a waveλm (nm often used)
⚠️ Coherence trap: Two separate light bulbs are not coherent — their phase difference changes randomly billions of times per second, so no stable fringe pattern forms. You need a single source split into two beams (or a laser, which is inherently coherent).
How the experiment works

The Setup

Monochromatic light (a single wavelength) passes through a narrow single slit, which acts as a point-like coherent source. This light then hits a barrier with two narrow slits separated by a small distance d. Each slit diffracts the incoming wave, producing two overlapping sets of circular wavefronts that travel to a distant screen.

Fig 2 — Overview of Young's double-slit experiment. Light diffracts through both slits; where the two sets of waves overlap on the screen, constructive and destructive interference produce alternating bright and dark fringes.

Why Fringes Form

At any point on the screen, two waves arrive — one from each slit. Because the slits are at slightly different distances from that point, the waves have travelled different path lengths.

Where the waves arrive in phase (crest meets crest), they add up — constructive interference → bright fringe.

Where they arrive out of phase (crest meets trough), they cancel — destructive interference → dark fringe.

The path difference determines which type of interference occurs at each point on the screen.

Constructive Interference

Path difference = whole number of wavelengths

Δ = nλ   (n = 0, 1, 2, …)

Waves arrive in phase → amplitudes add → bright fringe.

Destructive Interference

Path difference = half-integer number of wavelengths

Δ = (n + ½)λ

Waves arrive in antiphase → amplitudes cancel → dark fringe.

💡 Intensity at bright fringes: When two equal waves interfere constructively, the resultant amplitude is doubled. Since intensity ∝ amplitude², the bright fringe intensity is 4× that of a single slit — not 2×. This is a common exam trap.
Fig 3 — Coherent versus incoherent sources. Only coherent waves (constant phase relationship) produce a stable interference pattern.
Deriving the fringe spacing formula

Geometry of the Double Slit

Consider two rays leaving the slits and meeting at the n-th bright fringe on the screen. The screen is at distance D from the slits, and the fringe is at distance sn from the central maximum.

The path difference between the two rays is:

path difference = d sin θ

For a bright fringe (constructive interference), this must equal a whole number of wavelengths:

d sin θ = nλ   (n = 0, ±1, ±2, …)

When the screen is far away (D ≫ d), the angle θ is small, so we can use the small-angle approximation:

sin θ ≈ tan θ = sn / D

Substituting into the constructive condition:

d · (sn / D) = nλ   →   sn = nλD / d

The spacing between adjacent bright fringes (fringe n and fringe n + 1) is:

s = λD / d

This is constant — the fringes are equally spaced, independent of the order n.

Fig 4 — Geometry of the double slit. The path difference between the two rays is d sin θ. For small angles, sin θ ≈ sn / D, which leads directly to the fringe spacing formula.

All Key Formulas

Constructive:   d sin θ = nλ   (n = 0, 1, 2, …)
Destructive:   d sin θ = (n + ½)λ
Fringe spacing:   s = λD / d
Small-angle approx:   sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ (rad)
s ∝ λ s ∝ D s ∝ 1/d
✓ Exam strategy — proportionality reasoning: Many IB questions ask "what happens to s if you double D and halve d?" You don't need to recalculate — just use the proportionalities: s doubles (from D) and doubles again (from 1/d) → s increases by a factor of 4.
⚠️ Unit conversion trap: Slit separation d is often given in mm, screen distance D in m, and wavelength λ in nm. Convert everything to metres before substituting into s = λD / d. Remember: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m.
Graphs you must know
Fig 5 — Intensity vs. position for double-slit interference. The peaks are equally spaced (spacing = s). For negligible slit width, all maxima have the same height. Read s directly as the distance between adjacent peaks.

s vs. λ (straight line)

Plotting fringe spacing against wavelength with fixed d and D gives a straight line through the origin.

Gradient = D / d

Use this to find D/d from experimental data by plotting s against λ for several different colours.

s vs. 1/d (straight line)

Plotting fringe spacing against the reciprocal of slit separation (with fixed λ and D) gives a straight line through the origin.

Gradient = λD

Use this linearisation to determine λ from a range of slit-separation measurements.

sin θn vs. fringe order n

Plotting sin θn (where θn = arctan(sn / D)) against fringe order n yields a straight line through the origin with gradient λ / d. This linearisation avoids measuring small fringe spacings directly and is useful in high-precision experiments.

HL extension — finite slit width

Real Slits Have Width

In a real experiment, each slit has a finite width a. This produces a single-slit diffraction envelope that modulates the double-slit fringes. Some bright fringes may be "missing" where a double-slit maximum coincides with a single-slit minimum.

The condition for missing orders occurs when the ratio d / a is an integer — the m-th double-slit maximum vanishes at the k-th single-slit minimum, where m / k = d / a.

Fig 6 — Ideal vs. real double-slit pattern. The dashed curve is the single-slit diffraction envelope (from slit width a). Where the envelope reaches zero, double-slit fringes vanish — these are "missing orders".
Worked example

Worked Example — Sodium Light Double-Slit Calculation

2

s = λD / d
3

s = (589 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.80) / (2.5 × 10⁻⁴)
s = (1.649 × 10⁻⁶) / (2.5 × 10⁻⁴)
s = 6.60 × 10⁻³ m
4
State the answer with units:
s = 6.60 mm

Follow-Up — Proportionality Reasoning

(b) If the experiment is repeated with blue light (λ = 450 nm), the fringe spacing decreases because s ∝ λ. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than sodium light, so the fringes become closer together.

(c) If the slit separation is doubled to 0.50 mm (same λ, same D), then since s ∝ 1/d, doubling d halves s. New fringe spacing = 6.60 / 2 = 3.30 mm.

💡 Examiner's insight: Part (b) is a "state and explain" question — you must give the direction of change AND link it to the formula or proportionality for full marks.
Common misconceptions

5 Lesson 5 of 8 · C.3 Wave Phenomena
Multiple Slits & Diffraction Gratings
From two slits to thousands — understanding how increasing N produces sharp, bright interference maxima and the power of the grating equation d sin θ = nλ.

🌈 Why Does a CD Spray Rainbows?

Hold a CD or DVD under a white light and tilt it. You see vivid rainbow colours fanning out across the surface. It is not a prism — there is no refraction through a material. The tightly spaced tracks on the disc (spacing ≈ 1.6 µm) act as a reflection diffraction grating. Each colour in white light constructively interferes at a different angle, splitting the light into a spectrum. By the end of this lesson you will be able to calculate exactly which colours appear at which angles.

Fig 1 — A CD acts as a reflection diffraction grating. The track spacing is about 1.6 µm, comparable to visible wavelengths, so each colour diffracts at a different angle producing the rainbow pattern.
From double slit to N slits

What Happens When You Add More Slits?

In double-slit interference you observe broad, evenly spaced bright fringes. Now imagine adding a third slit, then a fourth, then fifty. The key insight is that the positions of the bright fringes do not change — they are controlled only by the slit spacing d and the wavelength λ. What changes dramatically is the sharpness and brightness of each fringe.

As the number of slits N increases, the primary maxima become much narrower and much brighter (intensity scales as N²). The broad humps of the double-slit pattern are replaced by tall, needle-like peaks. Between them, small secondary maxima (N − 2 of them) appear but become negligibly faint for large N.

Fig 2 — As the number of slits N increases, the primary maxima stay at the same angular positions but become dramatically narrower and more intense. Secondary maxima between them shrink to insignificance.
💡 Key idea: More slits do not move the peaks — they sharpen them. The grating equation d sin θ = nλ is identical for 2 slits or 2000 slits. The slit spacing d has not changed; only the number of sources contributing has increased.

Primary vs Secondary Maxima

Primary (principal) maxima are the very bright, narrow fringes whose positions satisfy d sin θ = nλ. Their peak intensity is proportional to N², where N is the number of slits.

Secondary maxima are the tiny bumps that appear between adjacent primary maxima. There are exactly N − 2 secondary maxima between each pair of primary maxima. For a diffraction grating with hundreds of slits, these secondary maxima are negligible.

Primary maxima: N² intensity Secondary maxima: N − 2 between peaks Peak positions: unchanged by N
The diffraction grating

What Is a Diffraction Grating?

A diffraction grating is simply a very large number of equally spaced parallel slits — typically hundreds or thousands per millimetre. Because N is so large, the primary maxima are extremely sharp and bright, making the grating an incredibly precise tool for measuring wavelengths.

Gratings are specified by their line density, for example "600 lines per mm". The slit spacing (also called the grating constant) is d = 1 / (lines per metre). Converting correctly from lines/mm to lines/m is critical.

d = 1 / (lines per metre)
⚠️ Unit trap: If a grating has 500 lines/mm, you must convert to lines per metre before computing d. That means d = 1 / (500 × 10³) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. Writing d = 1/500 = 0.002 mm gives the wrong power of ten and will cost you marks.

Deriving the Grating Equation

Consider parallel monochromatic light hitting a grating at normal incidence. Each slit acts as a coherent source. For a primary maximum to form, the waves from every pair of adjacent slits must arrive in phase at the screen. This requires the path difference between adjacent slits to be a whole number of wavelengths.

From the geometry, the path difference between adjacent slits is d sin θ, where θ is the angle from the central axis. Setting this equal to nλ gives the grating equation:

d sin θ = nλ

Here d is the slit spacing, θ is the diffraction angle, n is the order number (0, 1, 2, …), and λ is the wavelength.

Fig 3 — Parallel rays arrive at a grating. The path difference between adjacent slits is d sin θ. For constructive interference this must equal nλ.
Key relationships & proportionalities

Reading the Grating Equation

From d sin θ = nλ, three important proportionalities follow (each holding the other variables constant):

sin θ ∝ n — Higher orders appear at larger angles. The spacing between orders is equal in sin θ, not in θ itself.

sin θ ∝ λ — Longer wavelengths (red) diffract to larger angles than shorter wavelengths (blue). This is why gratings spread white light into a spectrum with red on the outside.

sin θ ∝ 1/d — More lines per mm means a smaller d, which pushes maxima to wider angles. A finer grating spreads the spectrum more.

Maximum Observable Order

Since sin θ cannot exceed 1, there is a highest observable order for any grating and wavelength combination. Setting sin θ = 1 in the grating equation gives:

n_max = floor(d / λ)

You must round down to the nearest integer because sin θ = 1 corresponds to θ = 90°, which is the physical limit. Any order for which nλ/d would exceed 1 simply does not appear.

✓ Exam tip: When asked "determine the highest order visible", calculate d/λ and take the integer part. Always show the inequality sin θ ≤ 1 as justification — examiners award a mark for stating this condition explicitly.
Intensity patterns & missing orders
Fig 4 — Intensity vs θ for a grating. Primary maxima are sharp spikes; secondary maxima are negligible for large N.
Fig 5 — The single-slit diffraction envelope (dashed curve) modulates the multi-slit peaks. Where the envelope reaches zero, orders go missing.

Missing Orders

Each slit has a finite width b, so the overall pattern is the multi-slit interference pattern multiplied by the single-slit diffraction envelope. A primary maximum goes missing when it coincides with a minimum of the single-slit pattern.

Single-slit minima occur at b sin θ = mλ. Grating maxima occur at d sin θ = nλ. Dividing these two conditions:

n / m = d / b

So if d/b = 3, the orders n = 3, 6, 9, … will be missing. If d/b = 2, then n = 2, 4, 6, … are missing.

⚠️ Misconception: "If 2λ/d < 1 then the n = 2 order must be visible." Not necessarily! The single-slit diffraction envelope can suppress it. The grating equation is necessary but not sufficient — the single-slit pattern is the "boss of brightness."
Graphical analysis

The sin θ vs n Graph — Key Linearisation

Rearranging d sin θ = nλ gives sin θ = (λ/d) × n. Plotting sin θ on the y-axis against order number n on the x-axis gives a straight line through the origin with gradient = λ/d. This is the most common data-processing graph in grating questions.

If d is known, the gradient directly gives the wavelength: λ = gradient × d. The y-intercept should be zero; a non-zero intercept suggests systematic error in angle measurement.

Fig 6 — Plotting sin θ against n produces a straight line through the origin. The gradient equals λ/d, allowing precise determination of wavelength.

Summary of Graph Types

GraphGradientUse
sin θ vs nλ / dDetermine λ from measured angles at known d
sin θ vs 1/dnλCompare gratings at a fixed order and wavelength
I vs θ—Sketch the intensity profile; label primary and secondary maxima
I vs sin θ—Linearised spacing; peaks are equally spaced at intervals λ/d
Applications

Spectroscopy — Identifying Elements

Diffraction gratings are the heart of the spectrometer, one of the most important instruments in science. When light from a hot gas passes through a grating, each element's unique emission wavelengths appear as discrete bright lines at specific angles. By measuring θ and applying d sin θ = nλ, the wavelengths — and therefore the elements — can be identified precisely.

This is how astronomers determine the chemical composition of distant stars, and how chemists analyse unknown samples. The sharper the lines (higher N), the more precisely two close wavelengths can be distinguished.

Fig 7 — Discrete emission lines from a gas discharge lamp viewed through a grating. Each line corresponds to a specific wavelength and can be measured precisely using d sin θ = nλ.
Trap corner — common misconceptions

❌ "More slits move the peaks"

The peak positions depend only on d and λ. Increasing N sharpens and brightens the peaks but does not change where they occur.

❌ "Small-angle approximation works"

Gratings produce large angles (30°, 50°, even 70°). The approximation sin θ ≈ θ fails badly. Always use sin θ exactly.

❌ "n = 0 shows a rainbow"

At n = 0 the path difference is zero for all wavelengths, so all colours overlap. The central maximum is always white.

❌ "More lines/mm = narrower spread"

It is the opposite. More lines/mm means a smaller d, which gives larger sin θ values and a wider angular spread of the spectrum.

Worked examples

Worked Example 1 — Finding Angles and Angular Separation

A diffraction grating has 500 lines per mm. Light of wavelength 550 nm is incident normally. (a) Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum. (b) Calculate the angle of the second-order maximum. (c) Determine the angular separation between the first and second orders.

1
Find the slit spacing d: d = 1 / (500 × 10³) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m
2
First order (n = 1): sin θ₁ = nλ / d = (1 × 550 × 10⁻⁹) / (2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.275 → θ₁ = sin⁻¹(0.275) = 16.0°
3
Second order (n = 2): sin θ₂ = (2 × 550 × 10⁻⁹) / (2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.55 → θ₂ = sin⁻¹(0.55) = 33.4°
4
Angular separation: Δθ = 33.4° − 16.0° = 17.4°

Worked Example 2 — Highest Order and Missing Orders

Using the same grating (d = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m) and wavelength (550 nm): (a) What is the highest observable order? (b) If each slit has width b = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m, which order is missing?

1
Highest order: n_max = floor(d / λ) = floor(2.0 × 10⁻⁶ / 550 × 10⁻⁹) = floor(3.63) = 3
2
Missing order condition: n/m = d/b. Calculate d/b = (2.0 × 10⁻⁶) / (1.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 2. So the missing orders are n = 2, 4, 6, …
3
Conclusion: Since n_max = 3, the only missing order within the observable range is n = 2 (when m = 1). The n = 2 peak is absent from the pattern.
💡 Examiner note: When explaining missing orders, always state both conditions — the single-slit minimum (b sin θ = mλ) and the grating maximum (d sin θ = nλ) — then divide them to obtain d/b = n/m. This logical chain earns full marks.
d sin θ = nλ d = 1/(lines per m) n_max = floor(d/λ) Missing order: d/b = n/m Gradient of sin θ vs n = λ/d I_max ∝ N²
