5 Lesson 5 of 8 · C.3 Wave Phenomena
Polarisation
How restricting the plane of oscillation proves light is a transverse wave — and the mathematics of Malus’s Law.
Core concepts — what is polarisation?

Why Only Transverse Waves Can Be Polarised

Polarisation is the restriction of wave oscillations to a single plane. This is only possible for transverse waves, where oscillations occur perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. Because transverse oscillations can point in many different perpendicular directions, a filter can select just one plane and block the rest.

Longitudinal waves (such as sound) oscillate parallel to their direction of travel. There is only one axis of vibration — along the propagation direction — so there is no additional plane to select or filter. This is why sound cannot be polarised, and why polarisation is direct evidence that light is a transverse wave.

Fig 1 — Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to propagation (multiple planes available for filtering). Longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to propagation (no plane to filter).
💡 Polarisation is one of the key pieces of evidence that light is a transverse electromagnetic wave. If light were longitudinal, polarising filters would have no effect at all.

Key Definitions

TermDefinition
Unpolarised lightLight whose electric field oscillates in all planes perpendicular to the direction of travel. Examples: sunlight, incandescent bulbs.
Plane-polarised lightLight whose electric field oscillates in a single plane only.
PolariserThe first filter that converts unpolarised light into plane-polarised light.
AnalyserA second polarising filter used to test the polarisation state or further filter polarised light.
Transmission axisThe direction along which the electric field component is allowed to pass through a polarising filter.
Fig 2 — Unpolarised light (oscillations in all perpendicular planes) passes through a polariser. Only the component aligned with the transmission axis emerges as plane-polarised light.
Fig 3 — The “picket fence” analogy: only the component of the wave vibrating parallel to the slits passes through. The perpendicular component is absorbed.
Transverse → can be polarised Longitudinal → cannot be polarised Polariser selects one plane Analyser tests polarisation
Malus’s Law — the master equation

Building Malus’s Law Step by Step

Step 1 — The polariser: When unpolarised light of intensity I₀ hits a polariser, the filter transmits only the component aligned with its axis. Since unpolarised light has oscillations spread equally across all planes, exactly half the intensity passes through:

I₁ = I₀ / 2

This factor of ½ is a fixed result — it applies every time unpolarised light meets a polariser, regardless of the filter’s orientation.

Step 2 — The analyser: The polarised light (intensity I₁, amplitude E₀) now meets a second filter — the analyser — whose transmission axis is rotated by angle θ from the polariser’s axis.

Step 3 — Vector resolution: Only the component of the electric field parallel to the analyser’s axis passes through. This component has amplitude E₀ cos θ. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, the transmitted intensity is:

I = I₁ cos²θ

Combining both steps for an unpolarised source:

I = (I₀ / 2) cos²θ

where I = transmitted intensity (W m−²), I₀ = incident unpolarised intensity (W m−²), and θ = angle between the transmission axes of the polariser and analyser.

Fig 4 — Malus’s Law setup: unpolarised light I₀ passes through a polariser (emerging as I₁ = I₀/2), then through an analyser rotated at angle θ. The final transmitted intensity is I = I₁ cos²θ.
⚠️ The most common exam trap: If the question states the intensity of unpolarised light, you must include the factor of ½ before applying cos²θ. If the question gives intensity after the polariser (already polarised), use I = I₁ cos²θ directly. Forgetting the ½ is the single most dropped mark on polarisation questions.
✓ Exam strategy: Always ask yourself — “Is this light unpolarised or already polarised?” Write down I₁ = I₀/2 as a separate line before applying Malus’s Law. This earns you a method mark even if you make an arithmetic slip later.
I₁ = I₀ / 2 I = I₁ cos²θ I = (I₀/2) cos²θ Intensity ∝ Amplitude²
Graphical analysis

Graph 1: Transmitted Intensity vs Analyser Angle (I vs θ)

Plotting the transmitted intensity I against the analyser angle θ produces a cos²θ curve. The intensity reaches maximum values at θ = 0°, 180°, and 360° (axes aligned or anti-aligned) and falls to zero at θ = 90° and 270° (crossed polarisers).

Notice the curve is not linear: at θ = 45°, the intensity is 50% of maximum (since cos²45° = 0.5), not 50% of the way to zero. This non-linearity is a hallmark of the cos² relationship.

Fig 5 — I vs θ graph: a cos²θ curve with maxima at 0° and 180°, and zeros at 90° and 270°.
Fig 6 — Linearised graph: plotting I vs cos²θ gives a straight line through the origin with gradient equal to I₁, confirming direct proportionality.

Graph 2: Linearised Graph (I vs cos²θ)

To verify Malus’s Law experimentally, plot I on the y-axis against cos²θ on the x-axis. If the law holds, the result is a straight line through the origin. The gradient of this line equals I₁ (the intensity after the polariser). This linearisation technique is a very common exam question — you may be asked to determine the gradient and explain its physical significance.

💡 If an examiner asks you to “estimate the angle at which the intensity is 25% of maximum,” use cos²θ = 0.25, so cos θ = 0.5, giving θ = 60°. Likewise, 50% of maximum occurs at θ = 45° (since cos²45° = 0.5).
Polarisation by reflection

Glare and Polaroid Sunglasses

When unpolarised light reflects off a non-metallic surface such as water, glass, or a road, the reflected light becomes partially plane-polarised in the horizontal plane. This is the source of glare.

Polaroid sunglasses exploit this by having a vertical transmission axis. Since the glare is predominantly horizontally polarised, the vertical filter blocks most of it, reducing glare intensity dramatically.

At a specific angle of incidence called Brewster’s angle (θp = arctan n, where n is the refractive index), the reflected light is 100% horizontally polarised. At all other angles, the reflected light is only partially polarised.

Fig 7 — Polarisation by reflection: unpolarised light strikes a non-metallic surface. The reflected ray is partially polarised in the horizontal plane. At Brewster’s angle, the reflected ray is 100% horizontally polarised.
⚠️ Misconception alert: Reflected light is not always fully polarised — it is only partially polarised at most angles. Complete polarisation of the reflected ray occurs only at Brewster’s angle.
Extension — the three-filter paradox

Adding a Filter Can Increase Transmission

Consider two crossed polarisers (axes at 90°): no light passes through. Now insert a third filter between them at angle θ to the first polariser. Remarkably, light now passes through the system.

The middle filter rotates the plane of polarisation. The polarised light emerging from the first filter has a component along the middle filter’s axis (I₁ cos²θ). This re-polarised light then has a component along the final filter’s axis [cos²(90° − θ)]. The resulting intensity is:

Ifinal = (I₀ / 2) · cos²θ · cos²(90° − θ)

Maximum transmission occurs when the middle filter is at θ = 45°, giving Ifinal = I₀/8. This paradox beautifully illustrates that polarisation is about vector components, not simple “blocking.”

Fig 8 — The three-filter paradox: crossed polarisers block all light, but inserting a middle filter at 45° allows light through. The middle filter creates a new polarisation component that can pass the final filter.
Worked example

Worked Example — Unpolarised Light Through Two Filters

Unpolarised sunlight of intensity 950 W m⁻² passes through a vertical polariser. It then passes through an analyser rotated 30° from vertical. Calculate the final transmitted intensity.

1
Identify the known values: I₀ = 950 W m⁻² (unpolarised), θ = 30° (angle between transmission axes).
2
Apply the polariser rule: The light is unpolarised, so the polariser halves the intensity.
I₁ = I₀ / 2 = 950 / 2 = 475 W m⁻².
Do not apply cos²θ yet — that is only used at the analyser.
3
Apply Malus’s Law at the analyser:
I = I₁ cos²θ = 475 × cos²(30°).
cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866, so cos²30° = 0.75.
4
Calculate and state answer with units:
I = 475 × 0.75 = 356 W m⁻² (3 s.f.).
Common misconceptions — trap corner

Misconceptions to Avoid

❌ Misconception✅ Correct Physics
A polariser creates polarised lightA polariser filters existing light — it removes the component perpendicular to the transmission axis. It does not create new light.
Any wave can be polarisedOnly transverse waves can be polarised. Longitudinal waves (e.g. sound) cannot, because oscillations occur along the propagation direction only.
I = I₀ cos²θ (missing the ½)This is only correct if I₀ is already polarised. If I₀ is unpolarised, you must write I = (I₀/2) cos²θ.
Reflected light is always fully polarisedReflected light is only partially polarised at most angles. Full polarisation occurs only at Brewster’s angle (θp = arctan n).
Real-world application — LCD screens

How LCD Screens Use Polarisation

A liquid crystal display works by sandwiching liquid crystal material between two crossed polarisers. A backlight shines through the first (vertical) polariser, producing plane-polarised light. The liquid crystal layer can twist the plane of polarisation by a controllable amount when a voltage is applied across it.

When no voltage is applied, the liquid crystals twist the polarisation by 90°, allowing light to pass through the second (horizontal) polariser — the pixel appears bright. When voltage is applied, the crystals straighten, the plane is not rotated, and the crossed polariser blocks the light — the pixel appears dark. By varying the voltage, intermediate brightness levels are achieved.

lessons.C.4__01__Formation of Standing Waves:
3 Lesson 3 of 5 · C.4
Standing Waves in Strings
How two travelling waves create a stationary pattern of nodes and antinodes — and the physics behind every guitar string, piano wire, and violin.

Question to Ponder

Why does a guitar string seem to "freeze" into a shape with multiple motionless points when you lightly touch it at the 12th fret? And why does a jump rope form a loop that stays in one place instead of travelling along the rope?

The answer lies in the superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions — producing a standing wave.

Fig 1 — Guitar strings vibrate in standing wave patterns. Pressing a fret changes the effective length L, changing the pitch. Lightly touching at the 12th fret forces a node at the midpoint, producing the second harmonic.
Core knowledge — how standing waves form

How a Standing Wave Forms

Imagine sending a wave pulse along a string towards a fixed end. When the pulse arrives, it reflects and returns inverted (flipped). Now picture a continuous wave: the original wave travels to the right while the reflected wave travels to the left. You have two identical waves moving in opposite directions.

These two waves interfere. At certain points, a crest from one wave always meets a trough from the other — they cancel permanently. These points of zero displacement are called nodes (N). Harmonics in Pipes
Standing wave patterns in open and closed pipes — boundary conditions, harmonic series, and resonant frequencies

🎵 The Big Question

Why does your voice sound like a chipmunk when you breathe in helium, but like Darth Vader with sulfur hexafluoride? The speed of sound changes — but your vocal tract (a pipe!) stays the same length. The resonant frequencies shift because f = v / λ, and only v has changed.

This lesson is about how the length of a pipe and the conditions at its ends determine which standing wave patterns — and therefore which frequencies — can exist inside it.

Fig 1 — A flute is open at both ends (all harmonics), while a panpipe is closed at one end (odd harmonics only). The closed-end instrument produces a characteristically "hollow" timbre.
Core knowledge — boundary conditions

Key Definitions

Node (N)A point of zero displacement amplitude — air molecules are stationary. Always found at a closed end.
Antinode (A)A point of maximum displacement amplitude — air molecules oscillate with greatest amplitude. Always found at an open end.
HarmonicA standing wave pattern whose frequency is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.
Fundamental (f₁)The lowest possible resonant frequency that fits the boundary conditions of the pipe. Unit: Hz.

Why Do Pipes Resonate?

A sound wave travels down a pipe, reflects off the ends, and travels back. For a loud, sustained sound (resonance), the reflected wave must constructively interfere with the incoming wave — forming a standing wave. Whether this "fit" works depends entirely on the boundary conditions at each end:

Closed end → a rigid wall. Air molecules cannot move freely here → displacement node (N).

Open end → air is free to move. Molecules oscillate with maximum amplitude → displacement antinode (A).

⚠️ The sine-curve diagram inside a pipe represents displacement amplitude vs position — not a transverse wave. Sound in a pipe is longitudinal. The curve is a graph, not a photograph of the wave shape.
Fig 2 — A tuning fork vibrates over a tube partly filled with water. As the tube is raised, the effective air column lengthens and resonance occurs at specific lengths where a standing wave fits.
Fig 3 — At a node, molecules are stationary (zero displacement). At an antinode, molecules oscillate back and forth with maximum amplitude. Closed ends enforce nodes; open ends enforce antinodes.
The big relationship — fitting waves into pipes

Building the Logic Step by Step

The pipe has a fixed length L. We must fit a standing wave between the boundary conditions (nodes and/or antinodes) at each end. Two key distances govern how standing waves fit:

The distance between two adjacent nodes (or two adjacent antinodes) is λ/2. The distance between a node and the nearest antinode is λ/4.

From these two facts, every formula in this topic follows.

Open–Open Pipe (e.g. Flute)

Both ends are open → antinode at each end. The simplest pattern that fits is one half-wavelength: A—N—A.

The general condition is:

L = n (λ / 2)   where n = 1, 2, 3 …

Rearranging for frequency:

fₙ = n v / (2L)

All harmonics (n = 1, 2, 3 …) are present.

Closed–Open Pipe (e.g. Clarinet)

One end closed (node), one end open (antinode). The simplest pattern is one quarter-wavelength: N—A.

The general condition is:

L = n (λ / 4)   where n = 1, 3, 5 … (odd only)

Rearranging for frequency:

fₙ = n v / (4L)   (n odd only)

Only odd harmonics (n = 1, 3, 5 …) are present.

💡 Why does a closed pipe sound "hollower"? The missing even harmonics remove a large portion of the overtone series, producing a thinner, more hollow timbre compared to an open pipe of the same length.
Fig 4 — Open–open pipe: the first four harmonics (n = 1, 2, 3, 4). Antinodes at both ends. Each successive harmonic adds one more node inside the pipe.
Fig 5 — Closed–open pipe: harmonics n = 1, 3, 5. Node at the closed end, antinode at the open end. Even harmonics (n = 2, 4, …) cannot satisfy these boundary conditions and are absent.

Proportionality Statements

These are essential for qualitative exam answers:

f ∝ 1/L   ·   f ∝ v   ·   f ∝ n

Longer pipe → lower pitch. Faster sound speed → higher pitch. Higher harmonic number → higher pitch.

fₙ = nv/(2L) fₙ = nv/(4L), n odd Node–Node = λ/2 Node–Antinode = λ/4 f ∝ 1/L f ∝ v

1

3

Resonance
What happens when a driver matches a system’s natural rhythm – and why bridges can collapse in a gentle wind
Fig 1 — The Tacoma Narrows Bridge in 1940. A steady wind, matching the bridge’s natural frequency, caused catastrophic oscillations.

Natural frequency – the system’s own rhythm

Every oscillating system has a natural frequency, f₀. It is determined by two things: the stiffness (springiness) that tries to restore equilibrium, and the inertia (mass) that resists changes in motion. For a mass‑spring system:

f₀ = (1/(2π)) √(k/m)

When you displace the system and release it, it vibrates at this frequency – these are free vibrations. In the perfect (ideal) case with no energy loss, the motion is simple harmonic and never dies out.

Fig 2 — A mass–spring oscillator. The natural frequency depends on the spring constant k and the mass m.

Damping – energy leaks out

Real systems lose energy through friction, air resistance, or fluid drag. These damping forces remove mechanical energy, causing the amplitude to decrease. Three important cases appear on a displacement–time graph:

Fig 3 — Damping types. Under‑damped: oscillations with exponentially decaying amplitude. Critically damped: fastest return to equilibrium without overshoot. Over‑damped: slow, non‑oscillatory return.
💡 Examiner insight: Critical damping is the most efficient way to stop oscillations – used in car shock absorbers and fire‑door closers. Over‑damping actually slows the system down.

Forced vibrations and resonance

When an external driver (e.g. a motor, a push, a vibrating base) applies a periodic force, the system performs forced vibrations. The amplitude depends on how close the driving frequency is to the natural frequency.

When the driving frequency equals (or is very close to) the natural frequency, energy is transferred most efficiently – the amplitude becomes very large. This is resonance.

Fig 4 — Barton’s pendulum demonstration. The lighter pendulum with the same length as the heavy driver (pendulum 3) resonates with the largest amplitude. Cones provide adjustable damping.
✓ Key exam fact: At resonance, the driver leads the driven system by 90° (π/2 rad). Below resonance they are in phase; above resonance they are 180° out of phase.
Resonance curves – amplitude and phase
Fig 5 — Amplitude–frequency resonance curves. With increasing damping the peak flattens, broadens, and shifts to a slightly lower frequency.
Fig 6 — Phase difference between driver and driven system. The transition sharpens for low damping. At resonance the phase difference is 90°.
Fig 7 — Energy–frequency resonance curves. When resonance is defined by maximum energy (rather than amplitude), all curves peak at the natural frequency f₀, regardless of damping.
⚠️ Common trap: Students often think the resonant frequency (amplitude peak) is exactly f₀. In fact, with damping the amplitude peak shifts below f₀. The energy peak, however, remains at f₀.

Worked Example — Resonance in a mass‑spring system

1
Known values: mass m = 0.250 kg, spring constant k = 25.0 N m⁻¹, negligible damping.
2
Calculate natural frequency: f₀ = (1/(2π))√(k/m) = (1/(2π))√(25.0 / 0.250) = 1.59 Hz.
3
Resonance condition: With negligible damping, resonance occurs when driving frequency fd = f₀ = 1.59 Hz.
4
Phase: At resonance the driver leads the driven mass by 90° (π/2 rad).

Resonance in practice

Resonance is both useful and dangerous:

Fig 8 — Microwave ovens use resonance to excite water molecules; MRI scanners detect proton resonance; tuned mass dampers suppress unwanted bridge vibrations.

Microwave ovens: the 2.45 GHz radiation matches the rotational resonance of water molecules, heating food efficiently. In MRI, hydrogen nuclei in the body resonate at radio frequencies in a strong magnetic field, producing images. The Millennium Footbridge in London swayed because pedestrians inadvertently walked in step with the bridge’s natural frequency – the problem was solved by adding damping.

Graph-based analysis – gong sound decay

The intensity of a struck gong decays exponentially. A convenient way to analyse this is to plot sound pressure level (in dB) versus time, because an exponential decay in amplitude gives a straight line on a dB–time graph. The slope tells us how quickly the energy leaks away.

Fig 9 — Gong sound pressure data. A drop of 3 dB corresponds to the sound intensity halving. The gradient of the best‑fit line gives the decay rate.

From the line L = 88 − 1.9t (where L is in dB and t in seconds): the slope magnitude is 1.9 dB s⁻¹, so the time for a 3 dB drop (half intensity) is Δt = 3/1.9 ≈ 1.6 s. If the background noise is 30 dB, the gong is audible for about 30.5 s.

f₀ = (1/2π)√(k/m) resonance damping phase 0° → 90° → 180° 3 dB = intensity half critical damping Barton’s pendulum

1 Lesson 1 of 2 · C.5 Doppler Effect
The Doppler Effect for Sound
Why does an ambulance siren drop in pitch the instant it passes you — even though the siren itself never changes its note?
Hook & Diagnostic

🎯 Hook – The siren that changes its mind

Picture yourself standing on a pavement as an ambulance races towards you, siren blaring. The pitch sounds high and urgent. The moment it passes, the pitch drops to a lower, almost disappointed tone — yet the driver hears the same note the entire time. The siren never changed; your ears did the interpreting.

Fig 1 — Wavefronts bunch up ahead of a moving source and stretch out behind it. Observer A (in front) hears a higher pitch than Observer B (behind).
💡 Diagnostic question (think first): A loudspeaker on a car emits a constant-frequency tone. Observer A is ahead, Observer B is behind. Which is correct? (A) Sound waves travel faster towards A. (B) The car moves towards A and away from B. (C) Wavefronts compress ahead and stretch behind. (D) Both B and C. — Answer: D. The speed of sound in air is unchanged; it is the wavefront spacing (wavelength) that changes.
Core Knowledge

📐 What is the Doppler effect?

The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency (and wavelength) of a wave when there is relative motion between the source and the observer. The key variable is not speed of sound — that stays constant in a given medium — but the spacing between wavefronts.

Emitted frequency \(f\) is the number of wavefronts the source produces per second (Hz). Observed frequency \(f'\) is the number of wavefronts the observer detects per second. The speed of sound \(v\) remains constant for a given medium (≈ 340 m s⁻¹ in air at 20 °C). Source speed \(u_s\) and observer speed \(u_o\) are measured relative to the medium.

Fig 2 — Stationary source: wavefronts are concentric circles with equal spacing λ. The observer receives wavefronts at the same rate they are emitted, so \(f' = f\).

📐 Case 1 — Moving source, stationary observer

When the source moves, each successive wavefront is emitted from a new position. Ahead of the source the wavefronts are compressed (shorter wavelength → higher frequency). Behind the source they are stretched (longer wavelength → lower frequency).

Fig 3 — Moving source: wavefronts bunch up in the direction of travel (shorter λ′, higher f′) and spread apart behind (longer λ′, lower f′).

In one period \(T = 1/f\), the source moves a distance \(u_s T\) while the wavefront expands by \(vT\). The apparent wavelength ahead becomes \(\lambda' = (v - u_s)/f\), so:

Source approaching observer $$f' = f\,\frac{v}{v - u_s}$$
Source receding from observer $$f' = f\,\frac{v}{v + u_s}$$
⚠️ Notice the denominator: when \(u_s \to v\), the observed frequency shoots towards infinity — this is the onset of a sonic boom. The formula breaks down at and beyond the speed of sound.

📐 Case 2 — Stationary source, moving observer

When the observer moves but the source stays still, the wavefronts remain evenly spaced in the medium — the wavelength \(\lambda\) does not change. Instead, the observer runs into wavefronts faster (or slower), altering the rate of detection.

Fig 4 — Moving observer: the wavefronts are still evenly spaced, but the observer intercepts them at a higher rate when moving towards the source.

The effective speed at which wavefronts pass the observer is \(v + u_o\) (approaching) or \(v - u_o\) (receding). Since \(f' = \text{relative speed} / \lambda\):

Observer approaching source $$f' = f\,\frac{v + u_o}{v}$$
Observer receding from source $$f' = f\,\frac{v - u_o}{v}$$
💡 Key asymmetry: For the same closing speed, a moving source produces a larger frequency shift than a moving observer. This is because sound has a medium — the medium provides an absolute reference frame. For light (no medium), this asymmetry disappears.
Interactive Slider Labs

💡 What to notice: At us = 0, f′ = 1000 Hz (no shift). At us = +30 m s⁻¹ (approaching), f′ ≈ 1097 Hz. At us = −30 m s⁻¹ (receding), f′ ≈ 919 Hz. The shifts are not equal — the curve is nonlinear.

🔬 Interactive Lab 2 – Moving observer, stationary source

Drag the slider to change the observer speed \(u_o\). The wavefronts stay evenly spaced — only the rate of interception changes. Emitted frequency is 1000 Hz, \(v = 340\) m s⁻¹.

uo = 0 m s⁻¹  |  f′ = 1000 Hz
💡 What to notice: This graph is a straight line. At uo = +30, f′ ≈ 1088 Hz. At uo = −30, f′ ≈ 912 Hz. Compare with Lab 1: for the same speed of 30 m s⁻¹, the source-moving shift (1097 Hz) is larger than the observer-moving shift (1088 Hz).
Graphical Mastery

Fig 5 — f′ vs us: the curve steepens dramatically as us approaches v = 340 m s⁻¹.
Fig 6 — f′ vs uo: a straight line with gradient f/v and y-intercept equal to the emitted frequency f.
Worked Example

✍️ Worked example – Train approaching a station

A train approaches a station at 25.0 m s⁻¹ sounding a horn of frequency 450 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard by a stationary observer on the platform.

1
Identify: The source (train) moves towards a stationary observer. We use the moving-source equation with the minus sign (approaching).
2
Data: \(f = 450\) Hz, \(v = 340\) m s⁻¹, \(u_s = 25.0\) m s⁻¹.
3
Equation: \(f' = f\,\dfrac{v}{v - u_s} = 450 \times \dfrac{340}{340 - 25.0} = 450 \times \dfrac{340}{315} = 450 \times 1.0794\)
4
Answer: \(f' \approx 486\) Hz. The observer hears a higher-pitched note because the wavefronts are compressed ahead of the moving train. As a check, the receding frequency would be \(450 \times 340/365 \approx 419\) Hz — lower, as expected.
Fig 7 — Geometry: the train (source) moves at us = 25.0 m s⁻¹ towards the stationary observer. Compressed wavefronts reach the observer at a higher rate.
Applications & Extension

🩺 Real-world: Medical ultrasound blood-flow

Doctors aim an ultrasound beam (typically 6 MHz) at a blood vessel at angle θ. Red blood cells reflect the sound with a Doppler-shifted frequency. The shift depends on blood speed and the cosine of the beam angle: \(\Delta f = 2f_0 \, v_{\text{blood}} \cos\theta \,/\, v_{\text{tissue}}\). By measuring Δf, doctors can map blood flow speed — a non-invasive window into the circulatory system.

✓ Examiner tip: If asked why the angle θ matters, state that only the component of velocity along the beam contributes to the Doppler shift. At θ = 90°, cos 90° = 0 and no shift is detected — the blood moves perpendicular to the beam.

🚀 HL Extension – Radar speed guns & the factor of 2

For electromagnetic waves where the source speed is much less than \(c\), the fractional frequency shift is \(\Delta f / f \approx v/c\). A police radar gun uses a round trip — the wave hits the car and bounces back — so the shift doubles:

$$\frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{2v_{\text{car}}}{c}$$

Challenge: A radar gun transmits at 20.6 GHz. A car approaches at 130 km h⁻¹ (36.1 m s⁻¹). What is the frequency shift? (Answer: Δf = 2 × 20.6 × 10⁹ × 36.1 / (3 × 10⁸) ≈ 4.96 kHz.)

Trap Corner

⚠️ Trap corner – common mistakes

MisconceptionCorrect view
"Pitch rises because sound travels faster towards the observer."The speed of sound in air is fixed for given conditions. What changes is the wavefront spacing (wavelength), not the wave speed.
"The Doppler shift is the same whether the source or observer moves at the same speed."For sound, the medium provides an absolute reference. The source-moving formula and observer-moving formula give different shifts for the same closing speed.
"When the observer moves, the wavelength changes."A moving observer does not alter the wavelength in the medium. Only the rate at which wavefronts are intercepted changes (frequency of detection).
"Doppler shift depends on the distance between source and observer."The shift depends only on relative velocity (and the speed of sound), not on separation distance. For uniform motion, f′ is constant at all distances.
⚠️ Most common slip: Using the wrong formula — applying the moving-source equation when the observer moves (or vice versa). Always ask: "Who is moving relative to the medium?" before choosing your equation.
Key Points
f′ = f · v/(v − u_s) f′ = f · (v ± u_o)/v v = 340 m s⁻¹ in air λ changes (source moves) λ unchanged (observer moves) Δf/f ≈ 2v/c (radar)

Doppler Effect and Light
Explore how tiny shifts in the colour of light reveal the motion of stars, galaxies, and even the expansion of the Universe.

🎯 Hook – The cosmic speed gun

A police radar gun can measure the speed of a car using reflected microwaves. Astronomers use exactly the same Doppler physics to measure the speed of galaxies billions of light-years away. A tiny shift in wavelength reveals whether a star is approaching or receding from Earth. The colour shift of light becomes a cosmic speedometer.

Fig 1 — Doppler measurements connect radar speed detection on Earth to the expansion of distant galaxies.
💡 Diagnostic question (think – then click) — If a star moves toward Earth, what changes about its light: brightness, colour, or the speed of light itself? Answer: the colour/frequency changes — the speed of light remains constant.

📐 Spectral fingerprints of atoms

Every element emits light at specific frequencies, producing a unique line spectrum. These spectral lines act like fingerprints that allow astronomers to identify the composition and motion of stars.

Wave relationship $$c = f\lambda$$

If the source moves relative to the observer, the observed wavelength \(\lambda\) changes while the speed of light \(c\) remains constant.

Fig 2 — Emission spectra produce bright lines, while absorption spectra show dark lines where wavelengths are absorbed.
$$\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c}$$

🌌 Redshift and blueshift

A redshift occurs when wavelengths increase because the source is moving away. A blueshift occurs when wavelengths decrease because the source moves closer.

Approximation for low speeds $$\frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c} \qquad (v \ll c)$$

This approximation is only valid when the relative speed is much less than the speed of light.

Fig 3 — Spectral lines shift toward the red end when receding and toward the blue end when approaching.
💡 Astronomers compare observed spectral lines with laboratory values to determine recession speed.

🔬 Interactive lab 1 – Spectral shifter

Drag the velocity slider and observe how spectral lines move across the visible spectrum.

Relative velocity = 0c  |  Shifted wavelength = 486 nm
💡 What to notice: Negative velocity produces a blueshift while positive velocity produces a redshift. Compare the observed shift with \(\frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \approx \frac{v}{c}\).

🔬 Interactive lab 2 – Classical vs relativistic Doppler

Increase the speed toward relativistic values and compare the classical approximation with the relativistic prediction.

Velocity = 0.1c  |  Error = 0%
💡 What to notice: At low speeds the curves overlap closely, but near \(0.9c\) the classical approximation becomes highly inaccurate.

📈 Graphs every examiner uses

Fig 4 — A linear increase in redshift with distance supports universal expansion.
Fig 5 — The gradient of the graph is linked directly to the speed of light.

✍️ Worked example – Measuring a galaxy's recession speed

1
Identify: This is a Doppler redshift problem. We compare emitted and observed wavelengths to determine recession speed.
2
Data: Laboratory wavelength \(= 587.6 \text{ nm}\). Observed wavelength \(= 612.0 \text{ nm}\). Therefore \(\Delta\lambda = 24.4 \text{ nm}\).
3
Equation: Use \(v = \frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda}c\). Substituting gives \(v = \frac{24.4}{587.6}(3.00 \times 10^8)\).
4
Answer: \(v \approx 1.25 \times 10^7 \text{ m s}^{-1}\). The galaxy is moving away because the wavelength increased.
Fig 6 — Comparing laboratory and galactic spectra reveals the recession speed.

🌍 Real-world: The expanding universe

Most galaxies show a redshift in their spectra, meaning they are moving away from Earth. Edwin Hubble discovered that more distant galaxies move faster, providing evidence that the universe itself is expanding.

lessons.D.1__01__Newton's Law of Gravitation:
1 Lesson 1 of 6 · D.1 Gravitational Fields
Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
Why does the Moon stay in orbit instead of flying away? The same force that pulls an apple to the ground reaches across 384 000 km of space — and its secret is an inverse‑square law.

🍎 Hook – the apple and the Moon

In 1666, Isaac Newton watched an apple fall from a tree in his garden. He asked a revolutionary question: if gravity reaches to the top of the tallest tree, could it reach all the way to the Moon? He realised the Moon is constantly "falling" towards Earth — but because it also moves sideways, it keeps missing and stays in orbit. The same force that makes an apple drop with an acceleration of \(g \approx 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\) also provides the centripetal acceleration that keeps the Moon in its circular path.

Fig 1 — Newton's insight: the force pulling an apple to the ground is the same force that keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth.
💡 Diagnostic question (think – then click) — The Moon is about 60 Earth radii away from us. If gravity follows an inverse‑square law, by what factor is the gravitational acceleration at the Moon's distance weaker than at Earth's surface? Answer: \(1/60^2 = 1/3600\), so \(a_{\text{Moon}} \approx g/3600 \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m s}^{-2}\).

📐 Newton's universal law of gravitation

Every point mass attracts every other point mass with a force that is:

• Proportional to the product of the masses: \(F \propto m_1 \times m_2\)
• Inversely proportional to the square of their separation: \(F \propto 1/r^2\)
• Always attractive — it acts along the line joining the centres of the two masses.

Newton's universal law of gravitation $$F = G\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$

where \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\text{ kg}^{-2}\) is the universal gravitational constant. The small value of \(G\) means gravitational forces are tiny unless at least one mass is enormous (like a planet).

Fig 2 — Gravitational forces between two point masses: equal magnitude, opposite direction (Newton's third law). The force on \(m_1\) is exactly the same size as the force on \(m_2\), even if the masses are different.

🌍 When can we treat extended objects as point masses?

The formula \(F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2\) applies strictly to point masses. However, it also works perfectly for real objects under two conditions:

1. The objects are uniform spheres — then all their mass can be considered concentrated at their centres.
2. The separation is much larger than the objects' own dimensions.

For a book on Earth's surface, the distance \(r\) is measured from the book to the centre of the Earth, not the surface. The Earth's radius is \(R_{\text{E}} \approx 6.4 \times 10^6\ \text{m}\).

Fig 3 — For a uniform sphere, all mass can be treated as if it is concentrated at the centre. The distance \(r\) is measured between centres.
Linking G to g — gravitational field strength $$g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2}$$

On Earth's surface: \(g = \dfrac{G M_{\text{E}}}{R_{\text{E}}^2} \approx 9.81\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\). This is the equivalence principle: inertial mass (in \(F=ma\)) and gravitational mass (in \(F=GMm/r^2\)) are identical to within 1 part in \(10^{15}\).

🔬 Interactive lab 1 – Exploring \(F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2\)

🔧 Real-world: "weighing the Earth" – the Cavendish experiment

In 1798, Henry Cavendish used a torsion balance with small and large lead spheres to measure \(G\) directly for the first time. Once \(G\) was known, Earth's mass could be calculated from \(g = GM/R^2\). This was called "weighing the Earth" — one of the most precise experiments of its era.

Fig 7 — Cavendish's torsion balance: small lead masses on a suspended rod are attracted to larger stationary masses, twisting a fine wire. The tiny twist angle reveals \(G\).
✓ Examiner tip: when a question asks about "weighing the Earth", it means determining \(G\) (or \(M_{\text{E}}\)) from a direct force measurement between known masses.

🚀 HL Extension – deriving Kepler's third law

For a small mass \(m\) orbiting a large mass \(M\) in a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force:

$$\frac{G M m}{r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r} \;\Rightarrow\; v^2 = \frac{GM}{r}$$

With \(v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}\): \(\left(\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}\right)^2 = \dfrac{GM}{r}\), giving:

$$\frac{r^3}{T^2} = \frac{GM}{4\pi^2} = \text{constant}$$

This is Kepler's third law for circular orbits. Newton showed it is a consequence of the inverse‑square law.
Challenge: Jupiter's moon Io orbits at \(r = 4.22 \times 10^8\) m with \(T = 1.53 \times 10^5\) s. Calculate Jupiter's mass. (Answer: \(M_{\text{J}} \approx 1.90 \times 10^{27}\) kg)

Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion

Projectile motion can be analysed by considering the horizontal and vertical components separately. The horizontal motion has constant velocity (no acceleration, ignoring air resistance), while the vertical motion has constant acceleration due to gravity.

Key Equations $$v_{x} = u \cos\theta$$

The total time the projectile stays in the air, \(T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\). The horizontal range, \(R = \frac{u^{2}\sin 2\theta}{g}\). Maximum height, \(H = \frac{u^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{2g}\).

1 Lesson 1 of 1 · D.2 Electric and Magnetic Fields
Electric Field and Strength
Invisible forces shape every bolt of lightning and every circuit — learn to map and measure the electric field that makes it all happen.

⚡ Hook – The invisible map

Sprinkle iron filings near a charged balloon and they shift into sweeping arcs — revealing invisible lines of influence that reach across empty space. Place a second balloon nearby and the pattern warps, stretches, and merges. You're looking at an electric field — the same field that steers electrons through wires, drives lightning to the ground, and holds every atom together. The field is everywhere; charges just make it visible.

Fig 1 — Two like charges repel: their field lines curve away from each other in the overlap region.
💡 Think first — If you placed a tiny positive test charge exactly midway between two equal positive charges, would it feel a net force? No — the two repulsive forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel. However, this is an unstable equilibrium; any slight displacement produces a net force away from the midpoint.
Core knowledge

🧲 Electric field lines

An electric field is a region of space in which a charged particle experiences an electric force. We visualise these fields with electric field lines — imaginary curves drawn so that at every point the line is tangent to the direction of force on a positive test charge.

By convention, field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges. They never cross each other. Where the lines are packed close together the field is strong; where they spread apart the field is weak.

Key patterns every IB student must recognise: a radial field around an isolated point charge (lines spread outward for positive, inward for negative), a dipole field between equal and opposite charges (lines leave + and curve into −), and a uniform field between parallel plates (equally spaced, straight, parallel lines from + plate to − plate). Field lines are always perpendicular to conducting surfaces — if they weren't, the component of force along the surface would push mobile electrons until equilibrium is restored.

Fig 2 — Three fundamental electric field patterns: positive point charge, negative point charge, and electric dipole.
ℹ️ On a charged conducting sphere, all excess charge sits on the outer surface. The field outside is identical to that of a point charge at the centre; the field inside is zero.

📐 Electric field strength

Electric field strength \(E\) is defined as the force per unit positive test charge at a point. It is a vector quantity whose direction is the direction of force on a positive test charge.

Electric field strength $$E = \dfrac{F}{q}$$

The SI unit is N C⁻¹. For the special case of the uniform field between parallel metal plates separated by distance \(d\) with potential difference \(V\) across them, energy conservation gives \(W = Fd = Vq\), and rearranging yields:

Uniform field between parallel plates $$E = \dfrac{V}{d}$$

This shows that V m⁻¹ is an equivalent unit for electric field strength. The field is constant in magnitude and direction everywhere between the plates (ignoring edge effects).

The electronvolt (eV) is a convenient energy unit at atomic scales. A charge \(e\) accelerated through 1 V gains exactly 1 eV of kinetic energy — so an electron accelerated through 3000 V gains 3000 eV, without further calculation needed.

Electronvolt $$1\;\text{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\;\text{J}$$
Fig 3 — Uniform electric field between parallel plates: straight, equally spaced field lines from + to −.
✓ Examiner tip: When a question gives voltage and plate separation, jump straight to \(E = V/d\) — there's no need to know the charge. This saves time and avoids errors.

🔬 Point charge field & combining fields

Coulomb's law and the definition \(E = F/q\) combine to give the field strength at distance \(r\) from a point charge \(q\):

Field due to a point charge $$E = \dfrac{kq}{r^{2}}$$

This is an inverse-square law: double the distance and the field drops to one quarter. The field points radially outward for a positive source charge and radially inward for a negative one.

Because electric field strength is a vector, fields from separate charges are combined by vector addition. On the line joining two charges this reduces to adding or subtracting magnitudes (with careful attention to direction). At off-axis points, use the parallelogram rule or resolve into components:

Resultant of perpendicular fields $$E_{\text{R}} = \sqrt{E_{1}^{2} + E_{2}^{2}} \qquad \theta = \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{E_{2}}{E_{1}}\right)$$
Fig 4 — Combining electric fields: the parallelogram rule gives the resultant \(E_{\text{R}}\) at point P.
⚠️ When combining fields between two charges, direction matters. Between two positive charges the individual fields point in opposite directions — subtract magnitudes. Between a positive and a negative charge the fields point the same way — add them.

Applications & extensions

⚡ Real-world: Electrostatic precipitators

Inside coal-fired power stations, flue gases pass between charged plates that create strong, uniform electric fields. Tiny soot and ash particles pick up charge and are driven to the collecting plates, removing up to 99% of particulate pollution before gases reach the chimney. The physics is exactly \(E = V/d\) scaled up to industrial voltages.

✓ Examiner tip: If asked to "explain" how a device works, state the field pattern first, then link force to charge using \(F = qE\) — this earns the "link" mark.

🚀 HL Extension – Millikan's oil drop experiment

By balancing gravitational force on a tiny charged oil drop against the upward electric force between horizontal parallel plates, Millikan showed that charge is quantised in multiples of \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\;\text{C}\). At equilibrium: \(qE = mg\), so \(q = mg/E\). Every measured charge was an integer multiple of \(e\).

Challenge: An oil drop of mass \(9.79 \times 10^{-15}\;\text{kg}\) is suspended between plates separated by 5.0 mm with a p.d. of 306 V. How many excess electrons does the drop carry? (Answer: \(q = mgd/V = 1.57 \times 10^{-18}\;\text{C}\); \(n = q/e \approx 10\) electrons.)

Trap corner

⚠️ Trap corner – common mistakes

MisconceptionCorrect view
"Field lines are the paths charges follow." Field lines show the direction of force (and therefore acceleration), not the trajectory. A moving charge can cross field lines.
"\(E = V/d\) works for any electric field." This formula applies only to the uniform field between parallel plates. For point charges, use \(E = kq/r^2\).
"Doubling the distance halves the field." The field follows an inverse-square law: doubling \(r\) reduces \(E\) to one quarter, not one half.
"The electronvolt is a unit of voltage." The electronvolt is a unit of energy (\(1\;\text{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\;\text{J}\)). It applies to any particle, not just electrons.
⚠️ Most common slip: Forgetting to convert cm to m before substituting into \(E = V/d\) or \(E = kq/r^2\). This produces answers wrong by factors of 100 or 10 000 — an instant giveaway and zero marks for the numerical answer.
